90-tyoaika-kuljetusala.title: The "90 working hours" rule: how to apply it in road haulage
90-tyoaika-kuljetusala.description: What does the 90-hour working time flexibility mean in an employment contract in Finland? A worked four-month example and practical tips for driver rostering.
90-tyoaika-kuljetusala.html:
Key takeaways

  • In Finland, the "90 working hours" rule means that, under section 28 of the Working Hours Act (työaikalaki), staff may work on average up to 90 hours more than the working time set in their employment contract over a four-month period.
  • The 90-hour flexibility always requires an express written agreement in the employment contract or in the applicable collective agreement; without one, the extra hours are overtime.
  • On a 40-hour working week, the maximum for a four-month period is roughly 866 hours, i.e. an average of about 48.75 hours a week.
  • A driver's working time also includes loading, terminal work, maintenance and waiting time, so in practice the EU driving and rest time rules often bite before the 90-hour ceiling is reached.
  • Unused hours do not carry over to the next period, but any excess over the agreed average at the end of the period is paid as overtime afterwards.

The "90 working hours" rule means that, on top of the working time set in the employment contract, work may add up to no more than 90 extra hours on average over a four-month period, under section 28 of the Finnish Working Hours Act. In driver rostering this limit acts as a ceiling, which the EU driving and rest time rules narrow further still. Below you will find a practical worked example and a rota calendar to keep you on the right side of the law.

What does the "90 working hours" rule mean in law?

The "90 working hours" rule is a flexibility arrangement agreed in the employment contract: working time can be agreed to be, on average, up to 90 hours longer than the working time set in the employment contract over a four-month period (Finnish Working Hours Act 8/1996, section 28). It is an average, not a fixed weekly working time.

The provision and its purpose

Section 28 of the Working Hours Act allows employer and employee to agree that average working time over a four-month period may exceed the contractual working time by up to 90 hours. The aim is to allow flexibility in seasonal or fluctuating work: more hours in the busy season, fewer in quieter times. The averaging reference period may be up to 52 weeks, but the four-month period is the most common yardstick.

The law therefore gives the employer no unilateral right to extend working time; it always requires an agreement between the two parties. This protects the employee where workloads vary unpredictably, and gives the employer predictability across the seasons. Without such an agreement the employer has to fall back on statutory overtime, which is more expensive and subject to stricter rules. The flexibility is thus a tool for keeping costs under control, provided both parties understand its terms and consequences.

When is the 90-hour addition open to agreement?

The addition always requires an agreement: either the employment contract or an applicable collective agreement that permits it. Without an agreement, working time cannot be extended on average. In haulage this means the driver's employment contract must state both the basic working time and the 90-hour average addition, so that rostering and payroll are lawful.

Once the working time terms are correctly set out in the contract, it makes sense to track them in the same place as the jobs and rest periods. RAHTIS is designed for small haulage firms where the owner does the planning: https://www.rahtis.eu/fi.

How does the "90" rule differ from the "40" and "75" working time figures?

The three figures mean different things. "40" refers to standard weekly working time: 40 hours a week, the starting point in most employment relationships. "75" may refer to the maximum for a shorter period, such as two weeks, or to limits agreed in sector agreements. "90", on the other hand, is an addition on top of the contractual working time: the average addition of up to 90 hours over a four-month period under section 28 of the Working Hours Act.

FigureWhat it refers toPeriodTypical use
40Standard weekly working timeOne weekOffice work, regular shift work
75Maximum or agreed hours for a short periodE.g. two weeksSector agreements, distribution planning
90Addition on top of contractual hours, as an averageFour monthsSeasonal peaks, busy periods, haulage season

Why the figures get mixed up

The confusion arises because all three concern the same question: how much work may be done. In a small haulage firm, weekly rotas and the four-month average run side by side, and a driver's timesheets easily blur the weekly and period levels.

A rule of thumb: at weekly level you look at 40 hours; at period level you calculate the 90-hour addition as an average over four months. When planning shifts, check the week first and then make sure the four-month average stays within the limit. A single week may rise to 55 hours if hours are cut correspondingly the following week. That is precisely the flexibility the 90-hour rule exists for. In haulage, peaks come irregularly, and a fixed 40-hour week is often hard to deliver without either the employer or the driver losing out.

When does the "90 working hours" rule apply?

The 90-hour addition is an exception, not the default. It may only be used where the employment contract or a local agreement expressly states that regular working time may be extended by up to 90 hours per four-month period. Without such an agreement, working time remains as defined in the employment contract.

Agreement requirements and the duty to put it in writing

The agreement to use the 90 hours must be made in writing, and by the end of the period working time must be brought back to the contractual average. The rules on defining working time and on shift work are found in sections 9–11 of the Working Hours Act 8/1996.

In haulage, the collective agreement may change the starting points, so check your own sector's collective agreement (TES) first before writing the 90-hour clause into employment contracts. Even a one-lorry firm should do this as soon as it hires: without a written agreement the driver's overtime is calculated on a different basis, and sorting it out after the event is expensive. The clause should specify exactly which four-month period applies and how the average is calculated. Alternatively the period can be a calendar quarter, but it is usually defined by season: January–April, May–August, September–December. This ties the flexibility to the nature of the business rather than to random peaks.

How is the "90 working hours" rule calculated in shift work?

Worked example: 4 months, 12 lorries

Take the basic case: the weekly working time agreed in the employment contract is 40 hours. The 90-hour addition under section 28 of the Working Hours Act is spread over the four-month period, so the maximum average for the period is about 48.75 hours a week (360 h divided by 7.4 weeks, added to the 40 h base). In practice the check is done on the total hours for the period: 40 h/week times about 17.4 weeks is about 696 hours, and the maximum is about 866 hours.

A concrete example: driver A works 200 hours in January (peak season), 180 hours in February, 160 hours in March and 120 hours in April (quiet season). That totals 660 hours, below the 866-hour ceiling. The average is about 37.9 hours a week, i.e. below the 40-hour base. Driver B works 220 + 220 + 220 + 206 hours over the same period, a total of 866 hours. The average is exactly 48.75 hours a week, which is precisely the permitted maximum. The differences between the drivers come down to how shifts are allocated and to seasonal variation.

Overtime and shift allowances in the same calculation

Month by month, the period breaks down like this: 17.4 weeks divided over four months gives about 4.3 weeks a month. If the driver's rota is 44 hours a week, about 189 hours accrue per month, and the four-month total stays within the 866-hour ceiling. Every hour of shift work counts in full, including hours that fall on a Sunday or at night.

Overtime and shift allowances do not change the 90-hour calculation, but they are linked to it: hours above the 48.75-hour weekly average are overtime, paid at the overtime rate, and the shift allowance is paid separately for every hour falling within shift work. So record three separate figures for each shift: hours worked, hours falling within shift work, and overtime hours. With these kept apart, checking the four-month period is a matter of simple addition, not guesswork.

How does the "90 working hours" rule affect driver rostering?

In practice, the EU driving and rest time rules often limit working time before the 90-hour ceiling is reached. Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 limits daily driving time to nine hours and sets the weekly rest requirements, which means long domestic and terminal shifts fill the 90-hour ceiling faster than long international runs do.

Combining driving and rest times with the working time ceiling

A driver's actual working day is longer than the hours spent driving: loading, terminal work, maintenance and waiting all count as working time. When planning the week, add up both driving and other work and compare the total with both the 90-hour four-month average and the weekly driving time limit. That way you can see which one constrains you first.

In international driving, the weekly driving limit is 56 hours and the fortnightly limit is 90 hours, but loading, unloading and waiting are added to working time on top. In domestic distribution, less driving time accrues, but terminal work and loading fill working time quickly. This is why the 90-hour four-month average is often reached before the driving time limits. The planner's job is to know which rule binds first and to allocate shifts accordingly.

How dispatch tracks the running total week by week

Keep the period total visible every Monday: working time used per driver, hours remaining in the period, and a forecast of the average for the rest of the period. When the running total approaches 90, move shifts to a driver with spare capacity or shorten the days. That way you avoid overtime liabilities arising purely from poor planning.

What are the most common mistakes in applying the "90 working hours" rule?

The most common mistake is using the 90-hour addition when no flexibility has been agreed at all in the employment contract or a local agreement. In that case the extra hours are overtime to be paid, and they do not count towards the flexibility allowance.

The second mistake is forgetting to balance the period: if, at the end of the four-month period, average weekly working time exceeds the contractual figure, the difference is paid as overtime afterwards. The third is calculating the shift allowance wrongly, for example by not applying it to hours that the 90-hour flexibility has pushed into the evening or night. The fourth is relying on a paper notebook: without proper timesheets you cannot prove the running total, nor spot an error until the driver claims compensation.

How to put mistakes right afterwards

The fix is to recalculate the actual working time for the period, pay any outstanding amounts retrospectively and document the procedure for future periods. The Finnish occupational safety and health authority requires employers to keep reliable records of each employee's working time and to retain them so that the basis for pay can be verified. For drivers, driving and rest time data supplement the timesheets but do not replace them.

If the error is only discovered after the period has ended, the employer must pay the difference as overtime. This can come as a surprise: at the end of the four-month period it turns out the average has been exceeded by 2 hours a week, and over 17.4 weeks that is about 35 hours per driver. For an eleven-lorry firm that is nearly 400 hours of overtime pay that could have been avoided with weekly monitoring. A regular check every Monday is cheaper than a one-off payout four months later.

How does a working time system help you comply with the "90 working hours" rule?

A working time system has three jobs: track the build-up of the 90 extra hours automatically over the four-month period, import drivers' driving and rest times directly from the digital tachograph vehicle unit, and warn you before the ceiling is reached. Tracking on paper or in Excel usually falls apart at the point, midway through the period, when you need to know how many hours each driver has left.

What RAHTIS covers and what it doesn't

RAHTIS brings dispatch, the freight exchange and driver management together in one place, so rostering and driver details stay in a single view. To be honest: RAHTIS does not currently perform automatic 90-hour period tracking under section 28 of the Working Hours Act. That should come from a separate payroll or working time system that calculates the totals officially. Use RAHTIS for planning and recording allocations, but make sure the statutory tracking comes from the separate system's reports.

Selection criteria for a small haulage firm

Ask for these three features before you buy: an automatic four-month running total report per driver, import of digital tachograph (vehicle unit) data without manual re-keying, and an alert before the ceiling is reached, not after. If the system requires separate licences per driver, ask for the total cost at the scale of 12 lorries before you commit.

FAQ

Can I use the "90 working hours" rule if it isn't mentioned in the employment contract?

No. The flexibility always requires an express agreement, either in the employment contract or in the applicable collective agreement. Without a written clause, the extra hours count as overtime paid at the overtime rate and do not go towards the 90-hour allowance. Check your sector's collective agreement first, and if it permits it, still write the clause into the employment contract as soon as you hire.

How many hours a month is the "90 working hours" rule?

It depends on the basic working time in your employment contract. Taking a 40-hour week as an example: the maximum for a four-month period is about 866 hours; divided by about 4.3 weeks a month, that comes to roughly 190–217 hours a month. The average over the period may rise to no more than about 48.75 hours a week, but an individual month may differ as long as the average at the end of the period adds up.

Does a driver's driving time alone count as working time in the "90 working hours" calculation?

Not on its own. A driver's working time also includes loading, terminal work, maintenance and waiting, so hours driven are always fewer than total working time. Add up both driving and other work and compare the total with both the 90-hour four-month average and the limits under the EU driving and rest time rules. Whichever limit is reached first is the one that decides.

What happens if hours are left unused at the end of the four-month period?

Unused hours do not carry over to the next period, nor are they converted into compensation. The period is a closed unit: by the end of it, average working time must be brought into line with the agreement, and the new period starts from zero. If, on the other hand, the average exceeds the agreed figure, the difference is paid as overtime afterwards.

Should the "90 working hours" rule also be applied to subcontracted haulage?

No. The "90 working hours" rule only applies to your own employed drivers, because it is a flexibility based on the employment contract or collective agreement. The working time and rostering of a subcontractor's drivers are the subcontractor's responsibility, and the subcontractor answers for compliance. Even so, it is worth making sure the partner's contract terms and timesheets are in order before you start working together.

alihankinta-pienkuljettajalle-vaihe-vaih.title: Subcontracting for small hauliers, step by step
alihankinta-pienkuljettajalle-vaihe-vaih.description: Get subcontracting under control in a 1–12 lorry firm: freight exchange search, quote, POD and payment tracking in one workflow, without the paper notebook.
alihankinta-pienkuljettajalle-vaihe-vaih.html:
Key takeaways

  • When subcontracting, you carry out the haulage on behalf of another company and invoice that client, not the end customer.
  • The POD, i.e. the signed consignment note, is the most important document, because without it the invoice often goes unpaid.
  • The contract should set out the payment term, the division of liability and penalties for late delivery tied to a specific time.
  • Four metrics are enough: punctuality, payment time, empty running share and a comparison of subcontractors on the same route.
  • One tool that combines load search, POD and payment tracking removes most of the manual record-keeping.

In practice, subcontracting means finding freight on a freight exchange or from your own customers, quoting, completing the job and then invoicing with a POD attached. This guide covers the whole chain, from posting your availability to payment tracking, for a small firm of 1–12 lorries that does its own dispatching and invoicing. Subcontracting is the quickest way to fill a lorry when your own customer base is not enough, which is why managing it is a core skill for every owner-driver.

What exactly does subcontracting mean?

In road haulage, subcontracting means carrying out transport on behalf of another company: the client sells the job to its customer, and you do it with your own vehicle and driver. The client invoices the end customer; you invoice the client. The same model works the other way round, too, when you can't cover a booking and buy it in from another haulier.

Subcontracting vs your own fleet work

Your own fleet work means your own customers and your own haulage contracts. Subcontracting is a faster way to keep the lorry full: you look for loads on a freight exchange such as TIMOCOM, or take bookings directly from a larger haulier. The risk is lower, but so is the margin, and you often have to wait for payment from the client rather than the end customer. Your own customer often pays within 14 days, whereas a subcontracting client may stretch payment to 30–45 days unless the contract says otherwise. For a small operator this difference is critical for cash flow, which is why negotiating the payment term is part of the bread and butter of subcontracting.

Who is the subcontractor and who is the client

The subcontractor carries out the haulage and is responsible for its own driving, its driver and their working time. The client looks after the customer relationship and pays the agreed price. The interface lies where the invoice and the consignment note change hands. RAHTIS handles both directions in one place, and you can apply to join straight away.

The client is also responsible for customer communication and for any compensation claims if the subcontractor is late. The subcontractor, for its part, is responsible for ensuring the vehicle is legal, insurance is in order and the driver is qualified. Keeping these two roles apart matters, because both liabilities and costs are split differently from those with your own customers.

How does the subcontracting process work, step by step?

Step 1: post your availability and search

Start by posting your own vehicle availability on a freight exchange such as Trans.eu or TIMOCOM. Include the route, vehicle type, capacity and when the vehicle is free. At the same time, browse return loads for your route to keep empty running to a minimum. Keep your search up to date: a load found in the morning is usually cheaper and better than what's left in the afternoon.

Update your search at least twice a day, because many clients publish new loads overnight or early in the morning. If you run a regular route, make the search recurring so that you see loads on that route automatically without browsing by hand.

Step 2: quote and confirmation

When you find a load, quote quickly but check first: mileage, waiting times, loading times and unloading. Price on real costs, not wishful thinking. Always get the confirmation in writing, even if you agreed it by phone first. A written confirmation can be a simple email stating the route, price, loading and delivery addresses and the schedule.

Make sure the rate confirmation also arrives before the job, not after delivery. If the client doesn't send it in time, insist that the job doesn't start without it: without a rate confirmation you have no written proof of the agreed price, and in a dispute it's your word against theirs, which leaves you in a weak position.

Step 3: transport and POD

Stay in touch with the client during the job and collect the POD (the signed consignment note) as soon as the goods are unloaded. The POD is the most important document, because without it the invoice often goes unpaid. If the delivery point won't give you a signed paper copy, ask for a digital acknowledgement or at the very least a photo of the unloaded goods and the recipient's name. Send the POD to the client the same day, not a week later: fast delivery also speeds up invoicing and payment. If the client uses its own TMS, check whether you can upload the POD directly to their portal so the paperwork doesn't get lost in an email thread.

Step 4: invoicing and payment tracking

Once you have the POD, send the invoice with the consignment note, the quote confirmation and any extra charges attached. Track the payment term actively: note who pays and when. RAHTIS combines the quote, POD and invoice into one record and shows unpaid invoices in a single list, so you don't need to keep a paper notebook of who owes what. The RAHTIS API documentation explains how the system connects to other tools if you want to export the data to your own systems.

Invoice within 24 hours of receiving the POD at the latest, because the longer you leave it, the more likely payment is to be late. Add late-payment interest and collection costs to the invoice so that they apply without a separate reminder.

What are the most common subcontracting challenges?

For a small haulage firm, subcontracting problems come down to four things: late deliveries, dispatch run on paper, separate logins to freight exchanges, and nobody knowing who is paying when.

Late delivery: what it costs

When a subcontractor's lorry arrives late, the cost doesn't stop at the driver's day. Your own customer raises a claim, you have to enforce the penalty clause against the subcontractor, and trust is lost. Without a shared schedule and event tracking, you only find out about the delay when the customer rings. In RAHTIS the delivery status is visible in a single view, and through the API the status can also be shared with the customer (API documentation).

The true cost of a late delivery is higher than a single claim: next time the job goes to another subcontractor, and a bad reputation spreads quickly in a trade where clients all know each other. That is why tracking late deliveries systematically matters: if one subcontractor is repeatedly late, the next request for quotation goes to someone else first.

Separate freight exchanges and a paper notebook

The typical set-up: TIMOCOM, Trans.eu and Teleroute, each with its own login, an outdated TMS and a notebook for recording who owes what. Every search and request for quotation takes three logins, the trail of a load is lost as soon as the paperwork changes hands, and when every subcontracted load lives in its own email thread, nobody remembers a week later which client the load belonged to and at what price it was agreed. The problem with a paper notebook isn't just lost information; it's also that nobody can say at the end of the month how much subcontracting was done, what the average payment time was or what share was empty running. Comparing payment times by client also becomes guesswork, even though that is exactly the information that decides who gets the next load and from whom you should demand payment up front. Without these figures you can't negotiate better rates or spot loss-making routes, which is why consolidating into one tool removes half of this work and brings the monthly figures back into view without separate bookkeeping: when the same tool shows searches, PODs and unpaid invoices in one view, the monthly review takes minutes rather than hours, and decisions are based on figures rather than memory.

How do digital tools make subcontracting easier?

One view across several freight exchanges

Without tools, looking for subcontracted work means logging into each broker's site separately: TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu each sit in their own tab, and quotes and messages end up scattered. A tool that combines a freight exchange with a TMS brings searches together in one view, where you can compare freight, route and return load without switching between five logins. When the same tool handles both your own customers' traffic and exchange subcontracting, you have one place that tells you who is doing what, and where. This visibility matters especially when a driver is on the road and you have to decide whether to take a new load from your own customer or from subcontracting. Without a single view the decision is guesswork, and guesswork leads either to empty running or to overbooking.

Real-time tracking and reducing handover losses

Another tangible benefit is real-time tracking, i.e. knowing where each load and vehicle is right now. Once vehicles and drivers have been entered into the system, every load moves visibly from quote to POD and invoicing, following the workflow described above: the rate confirmation comes in, the POD is requested on completion, the invoice goes out and the payment term is tracked automatically. This reduces handover losses, because empty running and the search for a return load become visible in good time and no load is forgotten when invoicing. RAHTIS is built for exactly this: trailer, container and load leave on time, and the phone stops ringing (RAHTIS).

In fairness: no tool replaces a subcontractor's own reliability, and real-time tracking doesn't work if drivers don't update their status. The tool reduces manual work, not responsibility. The driver still has to enter their status in the system, and if they forget, tracking shows the last known position, not the actual one. That's why it's important to agree a clear routine with drivers: status is always updated at loading and unloading, not "sometime in the evening at the hotel". Building the routine takes a week, but after that tracking works without daily reminders.

How do you choose the right subcontractor?

There are three criteria: reliability, working time discipline and vehicles. Always ask for evidence of previous jobs and check that the subcontractor's operator licence details and insurance are in order before the first load. Also check that the subcontractor has valid CMR insurance covering carrier's liability on international journeys.

Ask for a copy of the insurance certificate and check the sum covered: if the goods are worth €50,000 and the insurance only covers 8.33 SDR per kilogram (Special Drawing Rights, roughly €10,000), the subcontractor's cover falls short of the carrier's liability. As the client, that means you bear the difference. That's why checking insurance is just as important as checking the driver's licences.

The "50 working hours" rule and driver workload

A driver's hours are not just the subcontractor's problem: as the client, you are responsible for ensuring the load doesn't push the driver into excess hours or into their rest periods. The EU driving and rest time rules can be found directly in the EU legislation database, and it's worth requiring the subcontractor to provide a timesheet extract with every job. If they can't show the hours, the load isn't theirs.

Timesheets aren't just bureaucracy: if the subcontractor's driver exceeds their hours and gets caught, the whole job can be delayed by days, and you answer to the end customer. Timesheets are therefore risk management as well as compliance. Ask for them in digital form, not on paper, so you can check them quickly before handing over the load.

Cutting late-night admin and getting a real-time picture

Many small hauliers find return loads on exchanges such as Trans.eu or TIMOCOM (Trans.eu), but cutting late-night admin takes more: a real-time picture of where your own and subcontracted vehicles actually are. In RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/et) you can see the status of your own vehicles in a single view, so subcontracted capacity is only brought in when you don't have your own. An honest limitation: technical fleet monitoring, such as fuel consumption or tyre pressures, remains outside RAHTIS for now. Cutting late-night admin doesn't mean you won't work evenings; it means that in the morning you already know which loads have been delivered and which are waiting, with no guesswork. If three vehicles are on the road and one becomes free tomorrow, you can see at a glance whether to take a subcontracted job or wait for a load from your own customer.

Which tools suit a small haulage firm?

For a small operator three things are decisive: one login across several freight exchanges, invoicing and payment tracking in the same package, and a price that doesn't scale per driver. Below is a comparison on those criteria.

Comparison table

ToolStrength for a small haulierLimitation
RAHTISTrailer, container and load on time; the phone goes quiet when quote, delivery and payment tracking are in the same systemNot as extensive a freight exchange internationally
TIMOCOMLarge freight exchange and network across EuropeDesigned for larger operators
TelerouteTraditional load searchDoesn't handle invoicing or payment tracking
Trans.euWide range of loads and documentationGetting set up takes some work
LoadAppLightweight tool for managing loadsCoverage depends on integrations

Where RAHTIS falls short

To be honest: RAHTIS is not a freight exchange in the same way as TIMOCOM, Teleroute or Trans.eu, so if you're only looking for loads, searching a larger exchange is an essential addition. If your business is international contract haulage with large operators, a Transporeon-type integration may be more relevant. RAHTIS is strongest when you do your own dispatching and invoicing, source subcontracted work from an exchange and want "who owes what to whom" to be clear without a scrap of paper. RAHTIS's strength is managing the whole picture: when you know where the vehicle is, what it's carrying and when the invoice falls due, you can make decisions faster than a competitor hunting for information in five different places.

Which contract terms deserve attention in subcontracting?

Three terms matter most: the payment term, the division of liability and penalties for late delivery.

On payment, hold out for 14 days or less, and agree late-payment interest and reimbursement of collection costs. Also state who pays the freight exchange and broker fees, so that a scrap of paper headed "who owes what" isn't your only record. Check, too, whether the price includes VAT or whether it's added separately, and whether the rate is per kilometre or a fixed price per job. Writing these details down saves explanations later, when the invoice arrives and the total doesn't match what was expected.

On liability, specify whether the subcontractor's liability insurance covers the full carrier's liability, and agree how the excess is split. Include a requirement for drivers to produce their Driver CPC qualification card and working time records. Also define who is responsible for loading and unloading: if the subcontractor's driver has to unload alone and it takes three hours, who pays for the waiting time? Agree waiting times in advance: for example, two hours included in the price, then €30–50 per hour after that.

Penalties for late delivery should be tied to a specific time, not to a "reasonable delay", with the exceptions defined: congestion, weather and unloading delays at the customer's end. For example: "For delays of more than 2 hours beyond the agreed time, excluding force majeure, the subcontractor shall pay 5% of the haulage price per hour or part thereof." This is precise, measurable and easy to apply in a dispute. The alternative, "reasonable compensation", leads to endless negotiation in which each party interprets what is reasonable from its own point of view.

Tie the terms to practice: require the POD and rate confirmation for every job and attach them to the invoice, whatever tool you use. Without attachments an invoice is just an invoice; with them it is proof of performance, and proof speeds up payment.

How do you track and measure subcontracting?

Tracking needs only four metrics, and three of them come straight from RAHTIS records without any extra work.

Punctuality: how many collections and deliveries were on time. When every job is logged in the system, the percentage calculates itself at monthly level. The target is above 95%: if it's lower, either the subcontractors or your own drivers need a word. Punctuality is also a bargaining chip: when you can show a subcontractor that their punctuality is 80% while others manage 96%, the next request for quotation goes to someone else without lengthy explanations.

Payment time: how many days pass from the invoice and POD acknowledgement until the money arrives. RAHTIS tracks the days on unpaid invoices, so you can see at a glance who is late paying. An average of more than 30 days means either your contracts are too loose or your clients are struggling to pay. Under 14 days is a realistic target if you've chosen your clients carefully and your contracts include late-payment interest.

Empty running: how many kilometres you drive without a load. When searching freight exchanges (Trans.eu, TIMOCOM, Teleroute), always check for a return load before quoting; empty running is measured as a share of total distance. The target is under 15%: over 20% means route planning is lacking or subcontracted jobs are too often taken one way without a return load. Every percentage point of empty running comes straight off your profit margin, so this is a figure worth knowing precisely.

Comparison: compare subcontractors' prices and punctuality against each other on the same route. If one is consistently more expensive than the rest, the next request for quotation goes to someone else first. In the same way, compare your own prices with the market: if subcontractors are offering the same route 20% cheaper, either your costs are too high or your price is too low to compete.

These four figures tell you which subcontractors are worth keeping and which of your own customers pay slowest. A monthly review is enough: there's no need to track them daily, but knowing these figures at the end of the month makes the difference between being able to negotiate better terms or not.

FAQ

How much does subcontracted haulage pay on a freight exchange in Finland?

On a freight exchange, the price is set by competitive bidding, so there is no fixed list price. The margin left to the client is typically thinner than on your own customer contracts. The price depends on mileage, waiting and loading times, and unloading. Always price on real costs and agree in writing in advance who pays the freight exchange and broker fees.

Can I manage subcontracting without a TMS if I have fewer than 5 lorries?

You can start without a separate TMS, but the typical set-up is then TIMOCOM, Trans.eu and Teleroute, each with its own login, plus a notebook for recording who owes what. Every search takes several logins, and the trail of a load is lost when the paperwork changes hands. One tool that combines load search, POD and payment tracking removes much of the manual work.

How do I invoice subcontracted jobs and keep track of unpaid invoices?

Once you have the POD after unloading, send the invoice with attachments: the consignment note, the quote confirmation and any extra charges. Without the POD the invoice often goes unpaid. Note who pays and when, and track the payment term actively. RAHTIS shows unpaid invoices in a single list, so the paper notebook becomes unnecessary.

Do I need a separate contract with each subcontractor?

Yes, and three terms matter most: the payment term, the division of liability and penalties for late delivery. Hold out for a payment term of 14 days or less, agree late-payment interest and reimbursement of collection costs, and define how the excess is split. Tie penalties to a specific time rather than a reasonable delay, and require the POD and rate confirmation for every job, to be attached to the invoice.

How do I avoid empty running and find a return load?

Check return loads for your route before you quote, and keep your own availability posted on the freight exchange with the route, vehicle type, capacity and time the vehicle becomes free. A load found in the morning is usually cheaper and better than what's left in the afternoon. Once empty running is measured as a share of total distance, you can see it coming down.

cmr-rahtikirjan-hallinta-digitaalisesti.title: Managing CMR consignment notes digitally, step by step
cmr-rahtikirjan-hallinta-digitaalisesti.description: Managing CMR consignment notes digitally: e-CMR fields, electronic signatures, carrier's reservations and archiving, with a checklist.
cmr-rahtikirjan-hallinta-digitaalisesti.html:
Key takeaways

  • e-CMR is legal in Finland and the EU under the 2008 Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention, provided the system guarantees the authenticity and integrity of the document and the identification of the signatory.
  • Reservations, such as damage and qualifications in box 18, must be recorded before the consignee signs, because an entry added afterwards loses its evidential value.
  • In Finland, consignment notes are kept as accounting records for at least seven years under the Accounting Act, and the original electronic data is a safer archive than a PDF copy alone.
  • The electronic signature is tied to the signatory's name, role, time and location, which settles disputes over the time of delivery and shortens insurance investigations.
  • Start the switch on a single regular route and keep paper CMRs as a fallback for when the consignee insists on paper or the destination country hasn't ratified the Additional Protocol.

Moving the CMR consignment note from paper to digital can be done in Finland and the EU in three steps: choose an e-CMR-compatible system that covers the mandatory fields of the CMR Convention, then introduce the driver's electronic signature and carrier's reservations (box 18, damage and discrepancies) so that they keep their evidential value in a dispute or an insurance claim. This guide goes through the fields, the signature, the reservations and the archiving obligations with a practical checklist.

What is a CMR consignment note and which of its fields are mandatory?

The CMR consignment note is the document for international road carriage that confirms the carrier has taken over the goods and that a contract of carriage exists. Its content is defined by the CMR Convention, and the same form is valid throughout the EU, whether on paper or electronic.

Key fields under the CMR Convention

The mandatory fields are: sender and consignee, place of loading and place of delivery, description of the goods, gross weight, carriage charges, delivery instructions and date of carriage. The time the driver takes over the goods and the driver's signature, along with the consignee's entries on delivery, complete the document. The text of the CMR Convention is available on the UNECE website, and the Additional Protocol permits an electronic version.

What the consignment note proves and what it doesn't

The CMR proves the goods were taken over and in what quantity, but it proves neither the quality of the goods nor who owns them. Damage and reservations are recorded in the reservations box, and they determine liability afterwards. That is why the fields are best filled in carefully at loading, not afterwards from a spreadsheet. In RAHTIS, the job on which you record the CMR details appears directly in dispatch and invoicing (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi).

Is the electronic CMR (e-CMR) legal in Finland and the EU?

Yes. The electronic consignment note under the CMR Convention is governed by the 2008 Additional Protocol, which allows paper to be replaced by an electronic document provided the system guarantees the authenticity and integrity of the document and the identification of the signatory. Finland has ratified the Additional Protocol, so e-CMR is also legal for Finnish traffic and for cross-border journeys to other ratifying countries. In practice, both parties, the sender and the consignee, need to agree to the use of the electronic method.

The Additional Protocol and its requirements

The Additional Protocol does not prescribe any particular software; instead it sets requirements: the transport data must be tamper-proof, signatures must identify the signatory and carry a timestamp, and the data must remain available throughout the journey. If the system goes down or the data cannot be handed to the authorities at a roadside check, the method does not meet the requirements.

When to keep a paper copy as a fallback

When the customer or consignee doesn't use e-CMR, or when you're heading to a country that hasn't ratified the Additional Protocol, a paper CMR note is still the safest backup. Many small firms first use e-CMR domestically and keep paper forms in the cupboard for cross-border work. If you're weighing up the switch, you can sign up for a RAHTIS trial at https://www.rahtis.eu/sv/apply and test how your own workflow copes with an electronic consignment note.

How is the consignment note signed digitally during the journey?

The driver's signature on a mobile device

The driver signs the CMR on a phone or tablet at loading. In practice an electronic signature means a fingerprint, a PIN code or a signature drawn on the screen, tied to the driver's ID and a timestamp. Finland has ratified the e-CMR Additional Protocol, so an electronic signature is as valid in court as a handwritten one Finland's ratification details for the e-CMR Additional Protocol (Finlex).

The consignee's signature and the moment of delivery

The consignee signs on the same device or on their own device, to which the driver sends a signature request. The moment of delivery is recorded in the system to the second, which settles disputes about when the goods were delivered. If the consignee refuses to sign electronically, the driver can revert to paper or record the discrepancy directly in the system.

What the signature must include

The signatory's name, role (sender, carrier or consignee), time and location are stored with the signature. This makes it possible to prove afterwards who signed and when. In RAHTIS, signature events and their details are available through the API, so they can be linked directly to invoicing and job status tracking (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/api-docs). The signature does not replace reservations, but it locks them into the document unchanged.

How are CMR reservations (damage, discrepancies) recorded digitally?

Box 18: reservations and recording them electronically

Box 18 is the CMR reservations box: it records anything concerning the condition of the goods, the packaging or the delivery at the time of taking over. With an electronic CMR the entry is made directly in the system during the journey, and it is timestamped. In RAHTIS, reservations are recorded from the job's side panel, so the entry stays attached to that job rather than in a paper notebook.

Damage checklist: photo, description, witnesses

To preserve evidential value, follow the same routine every time:

StepWhat to record
1. PhotoClose-up of the packaging and goods, with the timestamp visible
2. DescriptionWhat is damaged, where and how badly
3. WitnessesConsignee's name and signature before the load is handed over
4. ReservationText in box 18 before the CMR is finally confirmed

If the consignee refuses to sign, record that in the same box as well.

When the entry must be made before signing

The reservation is recorded before the consignee signs the consignment note. An entry added after signing loses its evidential value, because the consignee has not seen or confirmed it. In an electronic system this boils down to one practical rule: inspect the load, record the reservations and photos, and only then sign. In the RAHTIS API documentation (https://www.rahtis.eu/en/api-docs) the entries travel with the job status, so the client can see them too without a separate phone call.

How long must a digital CMR be kept and how should it be archived?

Retention periods in Finland and the EU

In Finland, accounting records, which include consignment notes and transport documents as vouchers, must be kept for at least seven years under the Accounting Act (Finlex, Accounting Act 1336/1997). In the other Nordic and EU countries retention periods typically range from six to ten years, so always check the requirement in the customer's country before deciding how to archive. An electronic CMR is kept for the same number of years as a paper one.

Archiving: PDF, original data or both

A PDF copy on its own is the weakest option: its signature data cannot be verified later. It is safer to keep the original electronic document in a system that keeps the metadata and signatures unaltered. Many hauliers do both: the system holds the data, and PDFs are saved at year end as a backup.

In practice, archiving is best linked to the same place as dispatch and invoicing, so that seven years' worth of records don't end up scattered across different services. RAHTIS collects the consignment note, reservations and invoice on the same job, and you can find out more or request a demo at https://www.rahtis.eu/ru/apply.

What should you check before switching from paper to digital consignment notes?

Choosing a system from a small firm's point of view

Test the system on one of your own empty runs and jobs before committing: how many clicks does it take to create a consignment note, and does it work on a phone at the depot without a network connection? Ask for a written price per company, not per user – in a 1–12 vehicle firm, per-user pricing quickly doubles the cost. Make sure the system supports CMR reservations and archiving as standard, not as an add-on module.

Training drivers and customers

For drivers, one practice run is enough: signing, attaching a photo and recording a discrepancy. Tell customers and consignees in advance that acknowledgement will be by link or app, and keep the paper option available for the first few weeks. Start with one regular route, not all jobs at once.

RAHTIS, honestly: where it's enough and where it isn't

RAHTIS handles consignment note management as part of dispatch and invoicing: the job is published, the driver updates the status, and the POD and consignment note are linked to the invoice in one place. It is not a full e-CMR archive replacing a national electronic consignment note system, nor does it merge several freight exchange logins into a single sign-on. If you only need the freight exchange and your own fleet management in one place, it is enough; if you need an official e-CMR protocol for every customer, check that separately.

How does the digital consignment note link to dispatch and invoicing?

When the consignment note is digital, the same data can live throughout the job: order, dispatch, receipt and POD form a single chain that dispatch, the driver and invoicing all look at simultaneously. A paper CMR requires copying and re-keying at every stage, and errors arise precisely at those handovers.

The consignment note as part of the job life cycle

In practice, a job moves through statuses: published, assigned, collected, delivered, POD received, invoiced. When the consignment note is part of the system, the arrival of the POD can trigger the invoice directly, and an available drop trailer or return load shows up straight away without phone calls. The electronic signature is a precondition here, because the driver's and consignee's confirmation reaches the system immediately rather than waiting for the paper to come back to the office. The eIDAS Regulation provides a common EU framework for electronic signatures, on which confirmations between systems can be relied upon (EUR-Lex, eIDAS Regulation).

Documenting drop trailer and freight exchange jobs

On jobs taken from a freight exchange, the order, consignment note and POD are often in three different places. A digital chain keeps them in the same work queue, so documents can be traced even through a subcontracting chain. In RAHTIS the consignment note, POD and invoicing are built from the same job data, but to be honest: if your customer specifically requires paper, the system doesn't remove that obligation; it supports both side by side.

Summary: moving from paper to digital CMR

Break the switch into five steps. First, make sure the system you choose supports the e-CMR protocol and the mandatory fields. Second, try the signature on a single job before a wider roll-out. Third, make reservations part of the driver's routine so that damage and discrepancies are recorded during the journey. Fourth, sort out archiving: the digital CMR is kept in the system, but backups and the retention period are your responsibility. Fifth, link the consignment note to dispatch and invoicing, and the paper shuffle disappears altogether.

An honest note about our own system: RAHTIS handles job tracking and documents in one place, but full e-CMR signing during the journey is something you should verify separately for your situation. Start small, measure the hours saved each week, and only expand once paper and digital are running side by side without problems.

FAQ

Can a driver sign a CMR without a network connection or a smartphone?

Most systems support an offline mode: the signature and entries are stored on the device and synchronised later. If the driver has no smartphone at all, the options are a paper CMR note or confirming the driver's ID on an office device. Test the offline function on your own route before committing, because the signal often drops at depots and ports.

Will customs or an insurer accept a digital CMR instead of a paper one in a dispute?

Yes, if the system meets the requirements of the Additional Protocol: the document is tamper-proof, the signatures show the signatory and a timestamp, and the data can be handed over at an inspection. In a dispute, what decides the matter are the reservations, the photos and the to-the-second timestamps that e-CMR records automatically. Insurers value photos and a precise time of delivery because they shorten the investigation.

What do I do if the consignee refuses to sign electronically and insists on paper?

Go back to the paper form for that delivery and record the discrepancy in the system so the chain stays traceable. Tell the customer in advance that acknowledgement will be by link or app, and keep the paper option available for the first few weeks. Start with one regular route so that briefing consignees stays manageable and discrepancies don't pile up.

Can one consignment note cover a trailer swap or a drop trailer job with several vehicles?

A CMR is tied to a single contract of carriage, but changing tractor units doesn't prevent that: a change of driver or trailer is recorded as an entry on the same document. On a drop trailer job with several vehicles, each leg needs its own receipt and signature. Check how your system handles multi-leg journeys before bringing such jobs into the digital chain.

How much does introducing an e-CMR system cost a small haulage firm?

The price depends on the pricing model, so ask for it in writing per company, not per user: in a 1–12 vehicle firm, per-user pricing quickly doubles the cost. Other cost items are driver training, for which one practice run is enough, and any add-on modules such as archiving. Test the system on one of your own empty runs before committing, so that you only pay for a solution that works.

consignment-note-cmr-opas.title: CMR consignment note: a guide for small hauliers
consignment-note-cmr-opas.description: The CMR consignment note explained box by box: who fills it in, who signs it, and how a correctly completed note speeds up invoicing and the POD chain.
consignment-note-cmr-opas.html:
Key takeaways

  • The CMR consignment note is the legally binding document for international road carriage; it proves the goods were taken over and serves as proof of delivery for invoicing.
  • The carrier's signature binds them to what the note says, so the number of packages, their marks and condition must be checked before signing.
  • The consignee's signature is the POD that releases the invoice; without it payment is delayed and the burden of proof shifts to the carrier.
  • Box 3 determines the right of disposal and box 20 the carrier's reservations, so empty boxes shift the risk of a dispute onto the carrier.
  • The electronic e-CMR is a legal alternative to paper in Finland, but it only works if the consignee is on the system too.

The CMR consignment note is the legally binding document for international road carriage; it proves that the goods were taken over and sets out the terms of carriage and the division of liability between the sender, the carrier and the consignee. This guide covers the legal basis of the CMR Convention, all 21 boxes of the standard form one by one, and what each party's signature means in law.

What is a CMR consignment note and why is it mandatory?

The CMR consignment note is an international document for the carriage of goods that proves the carrier has taken over the goods and that a contract of carriage exists. At the same time it is the proof of delivery on which you invoice the customer and look for a return load.

The CMR Convention and Finland

The 1956 CMR Convention is binding on Finland and all the Nordic countries; it defines the content of the form and the parties' liabilities in the official text of the CMR Convention (UNECE). When you carry goods across a border, a consignment note is almost always required, and its signatures determine who bears liability for damage and delay.

When a CMR consignment note is not required

For purely domestic journeys, a domestic consignment note or other delivery document is often sufficient. The electronic e-CMR is also a permitted alternative to paper in Finland. RAHTIS handles the consignment note and proof of delivery chain digitally, and data protection is described in the RAHTIS privacy notice.

Who fills it in, who signs it and who is liable?

The sender's responsibility

The sender fills in the key details of the consignment note: the parties, a description of the goods, the weight and the delivery address. By signing, the sender confirms that the information given is correct and is liable for any errors in it. If the details of the goods are incomplete, the sender bears the consequences.

The carrier taking over the goods

The carrier's signature means they have taken over the goods and checked what is apparent: the number of packages, their marks and their condition. Hidden defects cannot be detected, so the carrier is not liable for them. When you collect loads from the loading bay, check the boxes before you sign, because your signature binds you to what the note says.

The consignee's signature and the POD

The consignee's signature is the proof of delivery (POD): it proves the goods have been delivered and accepted. Without it, invoicing stays open and you may be left waiting weeks for your money. RAHTIS collects the POD and links it to the invoice automatically, so you know immediately which delivery is complete and which needs a phone call (RAHTIS API documentation).

CMR form boxes 1–10: the parties and the goods

The top half of the form shows who is sending, who is receiving and what was loaded onto the vehicle. These ten boxes determine who can bring a claim and to whom the proof of delivery belongs.

Boxes 1–4: sender, consignee and right of disposal

Box 1 records the sender, i.e. the party that ordered the carriage, and box 2 the consignee's details. Box 3 concerns the right of disposal: normally the consignee may change destinations, but if another address is entered in box 3, the carrier follows that. Box 4 is reserved for the carrier and the vehicle, and most people also enter the trailer here.

Boxes 5–10: details of the goods and attachments

Boxes 5–6 describe the goods: their nature, marks, packing and number of packages. Box 7 is the gross weight and box 8 the volume in cubic metres. Boxes 9–10 record the documents attached to the consignment note, such as customs documents, and the delivery terms. The electronic CMR uses the same boxes, and UNECE maintains an up-to-date list of countries that have adopted the protocol.

Why the top half deserves care: box 3 determines who has the right to change the delivery address during the journey, and without an entry the consignee controls disposal. Boxes 5–8 serve as evidence of quantity and condition at the time of taking over, so a missing number of packages or gross weight shifts the dispute onto the carrier. Boxes 9–10 tie the customs paperwork to the consignment note, and if an attachment isn't mentioned, the carrier bears liability for any missing documents. RAHTIS fills in these boxes directly from the order, and you can explore the API in the Finnish-language RAHTIS API documentation.

CMR form boxes 11–21: carriage, charges and reservations

Boxes 11–21 cover the mechanics of the delivery: route, charges, modes of transport, vehicle and delivery terms. They are short, but this is where most after-the-event disputes arise, because the boxes are often filled in in a hurry at the loading bay.

Boxes 13–15: charges, VAT and delivery terms

Box 13 records the charges paid by the client: carriage, surcharges, duties and other items to be entered in box 20. Enter amounts clearly and show who pays each item. Box 14 is reserved for the VAT breakdown, and box 15 states the delivery term, for example in Incoterms form. If box 13 is left blank but the agreed carriage charge is invoiced later, enter "carriage forward" or similar so that the driver and invoicing have the same information.

Boxes 16–21: vehicles, reservations and time of delivery

Boxes 16–18 concern the vehicle and rolling stock: registration number, trailer and container. Box 19 is reserved for customs instructions, box 20 for reservations and instructions (such as temperature requirements or unloading sequence), and box 21 for the time and date of delivery.

BoxContentTypical mistake
13Charges paid by the clientCarriage charge not entered, leading to a collection dispute
14VATMissing on international carriage
15Delivery termBox left blank, term interpreted later
20Reservations and instructionsVerbal instructions don't make it onto paper
21Time of deliveryDate only entered afterwards

RAHTIS pre-fills these boxes from the order details, so the same transport data is visible to the driver, in invoicing and on the consignment note without separate copying. The same chain also works for cross-border jobs, as shown in the German-language version.

Paper or electronic CMR consignment note?

Both paper and electronic consignment notes are legal. The CMR Convention permits an electronic version, and Traficom (the Finnish Transport and Communications Agency) provides guidance on the use of consignment notes in Finland, so both are valid as proof of delivery.

The legal status of e-CMR

The electronic consignment note (e-CMR) complies with the Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention, and a signature has the same legal effect as on paper. The problem isn't the law but the fact that the loader or consignee may not be on an e-CMR system.

What works in practice in the Nordic countries

For a small fleet, paper still works: the driver gets a signed copy, scans it and sends it to the office. It's slow, and paper gets lost. If your customers are subcontractors found through TIMOCOM or Trans.eu, ask in advance whether they accept e-CMR. RAHTIS collects the POD and consignment note in the same chain for invoicing, but honestly: if the consignee insists on pen and paper, going electronic only gets you halfway.

What happens if the CMR consignment note contains an error or is missing?

A missing or incorrect CMR consignment note does not usually invalidate the contract of carriage, but it shifts the burden of proof onto you: if the goods are damaged, you have to show what you delivered and in what condition. In practice, missing paperwork shows up as late invoices and disputes over whether the goods arrived at all.

The most common mistakes on small hauliers' forms

Box 13 (carrier's reservations) is left blank even though the packaging was poor or the seal was broken. The consignee records the damage in box 18, and without a reservation of your own you carry the risk alone. Other typical ones: the description of the goods is written solely on the sender's say-so, package details are vague ("one load"), and box 16 is left blank, so special transport charges go uninvoiced.

How liability limits relate to insurance

The liability limits of the CMR Convention (e.g. a cap based on gross weight per kilogram) do not replace your insurance, but the insurer assesses the claim precisely on the basis of what is written on the consignment note. A correctly completed form is the cheapest insurance evidence you will ever get.

How does the CMR consignment note fit into day-to-day driving and invoicing?

When you drive and invoice yourself, the consignment note is three documents in one: the contract of carriage, the proof of delivery and an attachment to the invoice. The structure of the standard form supports this: boxes 1–15 say who is carrying what, box 18 the reservations, and the rest the delivery details, as described in the IRU's guidance on the CMR form. Without box 18 and the consignee's signature you have a journey, but no proof of delivery.

POD, rate confirmation and invoice in one chain

In practice, the POD, rate confirmation and invoice form a chain: the rate confirmation shows the price, the consignment note shows what was carried and box 20 the carrier's reservations, and the consignee's signature releases the invoice. When these three documents are together, the paper "who owes what" notebook becomes unnecessary. Clear handwriting pays: an illegible signature or a missing date is the most common reason for late payment.

Subcontracting from a freight exchange: whose CMR?

When you take a load from TIMOCOM, Trans.eu or Teleroute, the client usually provides its own consignment note on which you are entered as the carrier. Check box 16: your company must appear there if you want your own liability and your own invoice for the freight exchange booking. Keep a copy yourself: if the client disputes the delivery, your signature on the consignment note is your only evidence.

How does RAHTIS handle the consignment note and proof of delivery chain?

RAHTIS joins up the chain that currently lives on paper and in email: consignment note, POD and invoice. The driver fills in the CMR boxes on a phone and sends it for signature, and when the POD comes back, RAHTIS assembles the consignment note, proof of delivery and rate confirmation as attachments to the invoice. The number of days an invoice has been unpaid is visible directly, so the "who owes what" notebook goes. Jobs for your own customers and subcontracted load board work run through the same pipeline.

What RAHTIS doesn't do (yet)

RAHTIS is not a load board: TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu searches stay behind their own logins, and you carry the load details across by hand. An electronic CMR with signatures only works when the consignee is on board too; an old-fashioned consignee means paper alongside. And if you're thinking of switching from McLeod, RAHTIS isn't built on that scale; it's made for the day-to-day running of 1–12 vehicles.

FAQ

Can the sender or a broker fill in the CMR consignment note instead of the carrier?

Yes. The sender fills in the key details of the consignment note and is responsible for their accuracy. A broker or client may also provide a ready-made consignment note on which you are entered as the carrier. Your liability is limited to what you sign: check the number of packages, their marks and condition before signing, because your signature binds you to what the note says.

What is box 11 (declarations) on the CMR and when is it mandatory?

Box 11 is reserved for the sender's declarations, i.e. instructions on handling the goods during carriage. It isn't mandatory for every journey, but if the goods need special handling, such as temperature requirements or a specific unloading sequence, the instructions must be on paper. Verbal instructions don't appear on the consignment note, so an unrecorded instruction shifts the risk of a dispute onto you.

How many originals and copies of the CMR form are needed?

The standard form comprises one original for the carrier, one for the consignee and one for the sender, plus copies for other parties. For a small haulier, the most important ones are the copy that travels with you and the proof of delivery signed by the consignee. Keep a copy yourself, because if the client disputes the delivery, the signed consignment note is your only evidence.

Can a CMR consignment note be corrected afterwards if I spot a mistake?

A mistake can be corrected, but the correction must be agreed by all parties and be traceable. A private amendment made in pen without signatures loses its evidential value in a dispute. If you spot the mistake before signing, correct it immediately. If the consignee has already recorded reservations, add your own remark and ask for it to be confirmed.

Is a photographed POD without a signed CMR acceptable for invoicing?

A photo can support an invoice, but it does not replace a signed proof of delivery. Without the consignee's signature, invoicing stays open and the burden of proof shifts to you: you have to show what you delivered and in what condition. Best practice is to scan the signed paper and attach it to the invoice together with the photos.

kuljettajan-tyoaikojen-seuranta-lain-vaa.title: Recording drivers' working time to meet legal requirements
kuljettajan-tyoaikojen-seuranta-lain-vaa.description: Recording drivers' working time as Finnish law requires: log hours, overtime and breaks correctly and avoid inspection problems. Checklist and example included.
kuljettajan-tyoaikojen-seuranta-lain-vaa.html:
Key takeaways

  • Working time records must be kept for at least two years, but keeping them for three years also covers late compensation claims.
  • Tachograph data alone is not enough as working time records; it has to be combined with timesheets and job orders.
  • Responsibility for recording always lies with the employer, even if the recording is done externally or by the driver.
  • The driver card must be downloaded at least every 28 days, so that data isn't overwritten by newer data and lost for good.
  • Overtime must be recorded separately during the shift itself, because it feeds directly into the payslip and your readiness for inspection.

Recording drivers' working time in line with legal requirements means logging driving, other work, breaks and periods of availability for each driver in your working time records, in accordance with the Finnish working time legislation for drivers (445/2019) and EU Directive 2002/15/EC, and keeping those records for at least two years. This guide brings both pieces of legislation together into one checklist, with an example job, including empty running, loading and breaks, logged line by line.

What does the law require when recording drivers' working time?

Recording drivers' working time is based on two pieces of legislation, which set both the limits and the recording obligation. Below is a brief summary of each, and of who is responsible.

The Finnish Drivers' Working Time Act 445/2019

The Finnish Act on the working and rest times of vehicle drivers (445/2019, Finlex) applies to drivers in commercial road transport. It requires the employer to keep working time records showing hours worked, overtime and breaks. The same Act sets the retention periods and the maximum working time limits. The Act came into force in 2020 and replaced the previous drivers' working time act. As the Act is Finland's national implementation of an EU directive, its requirements are in line with other Member States, but the detailed maximum limits may differ.

EU Working Time Directive 2002/15/EC

Directive 2002/15/EC harmonises the working time rules for drivers across the EU. Finnish law was drafted on its basis, so the Directive's requirements are reflected directly in the domestic recording obligation. The Directive sets minimum requirements, such as maximum weekly working time and minimum rest, but leaves the details to national legislation. This means that if you run cross-border international traffic, you need to know both Finnish law and the corresponding rules in the destination country.

The employer's and the driver's responsibilities

Responsibility for recording lies with the employer, i.e. you, even if you also do driving work yourself. The driver's job is to report their working time correctly. When recording is in order, a single system holding the data is enough at an inspection, just as RAHTIS brings jobs and their details together in one place. The employer's responsibility also extends to making sure the driver understands their reporting obligation: if the driver doesn't report working time correctly, the penalty still falls on the employer. That is why it's important to give drivers clear instructions and a recording template that minimises human error.

What information must be entered in the working time records?

Mandatory information

For every shift, at least the following must be recorded for drivers' working time records to meet the legal requirements (Act 445/2019 and Directive 2002/15/EC):

ItemExample
Driver's name and vehicle registration numberMatti M., ABC-123
Start and finish time of the shift06:00–18:30
Working time and overtime shown separately9 h working time, 2 h overtime
Breaks and their duration45 min break, 11:30–12:15
Periods of availability and standby3 h waiting at the loading point
Time off and job alternation leave18:30–06:00

Overtime must be recorded separately, because it has its own maximum limits and must be compensated. Periods of availability, such as waiting at the loading point, count as work even when the driver isn't driving. The records must also show the driver's working time category and any exceptional arrangements that have been applied. For example, regular working time and split working time are recorded separately because their overtime thresholds are calculated differently.

Where the data comes from: tachograph, timesheets and other documentation

Tachograph data shows driving, breaks and other work, but it doesn't cover everything. Shift start and finish times, periods of availability and information reported by the driver come from the timesheet or a system entry. In practice you need three sources combined: tachograph printouts, the timesheet and the job orders. Driver card data gives precise times, but it doesn't tell you whether a period was loading, unloading or empty running. The job orders show what the driver was supposed to do, but not always when they did it. The timesheet or system entry is the glue that joins the two together and produces the statutory working time records.

A worked recording example for one shift

Monday: start at 06:00, drop trailer collected at 07:00, 45-minute break at 11:30, consignment note signed at destination at 16:00, return load unloaded at 17:30, shift ends at 18:30. What gets recorded: 9 h working time, 2 h overtime, 45 min break and 1 h of availability at the loading point. When jobs and records run in the same system, as in RAHTIS, the job times and the records sit in the same chain (RAHTIS – Transportledning och lastbörs).

Broken down in more detail, the working day looks like this: 06:00–07:00 is other work, covering vehicle checks and driving to the collection. 07:00–11:30 is driving time, of which the tachograph records 4.5 hours of continuous driving. 11:30–12:15 is the statutory 45-minute break. 12:15–16:00 is driving time, including a short refuelling stop.

16:00–17:30 is unloading and waiting, of which unloading is other work and waiting is availability. 17:30–18:30 is the return drive to the employer's yard and vehicle maintenance. This breakdown is what an inspector wants to see.

How long must working time data be kept?

Retention period for working time records

Working time records must be kept for at least two years. This applies to all recorded data: hours worked, overtime and breaks. The EU Working Time Directive 2002/15/EC requires Member States to ensure that employers keep records of overtime and make them available to the enforcement authorities. In practice it is wise to keep the records for longer than the minimum, because a retrospective claim may come later. For example, a driver may claim overtime pay after the event, and without records you have no evidence of what happened. Keeping records for three years is a safe practice that also covers any late claims.

Retention period for tachograph charts and data

Tachograph printouts and downloaded digital data must be kept for at least one year. If the data is used as the basis for working time records, the same two-year retention obligation applies to it as well. Storing data systematically, for example in a RAHTIS-type system whose interface specifications are in the API documentation, removes the risk of paper charts going missing. Digital data must be kept in its original format, i.e. .ddd and .v1b files must not be edited. If you edit the files, they lose their evidential value at an inspection. That is why it's important to download the card regularly and store the data in a locked archive that only authorised users can access.

What are the limits on working time, overtime and breaks?

Daily and weekly working time

The Finnish Drivers' Working Time Act (445/2019) sets its own limits, some of which are stricter than in other sectors. Daily working time may not exceed 15 hours, and this covers loading, unloading, maintenance and waiting as well as driving. Weekly working time is 40 hours on average, calculated over a four-month reference period, so an individual week can be longer as long as the average stays within the limit. Under the general working time rules a week may not exceed 48 hours, and no more than 180 hours of overtime may accrue in a calendar year. These limits are worth writing straight into your own checklist, so that recording drivers' working time in line with the law becomes routine rather than a separate project.

Overtime limits and compensation

Overtime is only permitted with the driver's consent and is recorded separately from regular working time. Overtime is paid at an enhanced rate or compensated with time off, so how it's broken down in the records feeds directly into the payslip. The overtime threshold for regular working time is eight hours a day or 40 hours a week. For split working time the overtime threshold is nine hours a day. Overtime pay is at least 50 per cent of the hourly wage, but the collective agreement may provide for a higher rate. Record overtime separately during the shift itself and don't leave it to be fixed in the monthly routine, because then the driver doesn't know what their pay is based on.

Breaks and rest periods

A working day of more than six hours must include a break of at least 45 minutes, which may be split into two parts (at least 15 and 30 minutes). Daily rest must be at least 11 hours and weekly rest 45 hours. Daily rest may be reduced to nine hours three times a week if the driver returns home or to a place designated by the employer. Weekly rest may be reduced to 36 hours, but compensating rest must then be given the following week. These exceptions must be recorded separately so that the inspector can see when reduced rest was applied and whether it complied with the rules.

How do you combine tachograph data with working time records?

The tachograph records the hours driven, but working time records need more: working time subject to monitoring, breaks and periods of availability must be derived from the card data and supplemented manually. For driving and rest times, the source data are on the card directly in line with Regulation (EC) No 561/2006, but records meeting the working time legislation only come into being once that data is combined with information on loading and other work. Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 sets driving and rest time limits that are separate from the working time limits. Under the Regulation, continuous driving time is limited to 4.5 hours, and daily driving time to 9 hours, extendable to 10 hours twice a week. These limits apply only to driving, whereas Act 445/2019 covers all work, including loading, unloading and waiting.

Downloading the card and the vehicle unit

Download the driver card at least every 28 days and the vehicle unit at least every 90 days. Import the data into software that reads .v1b and .ddd files directly, such as via the RAHTIS API. That way the card data doesn't stay as PDF printouts but flows straight into your working time records. If you don't download the card within 28 days, it starts overwriting the oldest data with newer data, and you lose information for good. That is why card downloads should be set as a calendar reminder, not left to the driver's discretion.

Interpreting anomalies: empty running, loading and waiting

The tachograph doesn't distinguish empty running or loading. Mark them by hand: empty running at the start of the drive, loading as the start of work, waiting as a period of availability. Without a note, the inspector will treat unclear periods as working time, which costs you. For example, if the driver spends two hours at the loading point, the tachograph will show either "other work" or "break" depending on what the driver selected. If the driver selected break but was actually loading, the working time records end up wrong. Correct these anomalies in the monthly routine by comparing job orders with the card data.

Monthly routine for a small firm

Go through drivers' cards every month: compare the hours on the card with the records, correct anomalies and save everything before the start of the following month. The monthly routine is when you notice if a driver has recorded breaks that weren't taken, or if overtime is missing. Allow 30 minutes per driver for the routine. If there are many anomalies, retrain the driver on how to record. Don't leave corrections until the following month, because then errors pile up and become harder to fix.

What happens if recording is inadequate?

Inspections and authorities
