In Finland, occupational safety and health enforcement is the responsibility of the Regional State Administrative Agencies (AVI), and at an inspection you may be asked for working time records, tachograph data and employment contracts. If records are missing or incomplete, that in itself is a breach of the law, even if the driver's working hours were otherwise within the rules. An inspection can lead to written notices or obligations with deadlines, and the matter may end up being put right afterwards by an employers' association or a lawyer, at greater cost. An AVI inspection may be announced in advance or unannounced. Unannounced inspections often target firms whose operations have attracted attention, for example through lots of overtime or short rest periods. That is why records must always be up to date, not just when an inspection looms.

Duty to correct and the driver's rights

Inadequate recording often ends up costing the driver: overtime, days off and rest periods aren't realised if they aren't recorded. The driver has the right to claim for working time retrospectively within a reasonable period, and a claim may even be made for periods years in the past. Correct the records before an inspection, not during it. If a driver claims compensation after the event and you have no records showing that no overtime was worked, the burden of proof shifts to you. This means you may have to pay compensation even if the overtime was never actually worked. That is why the records protect both driver and employer.

How should working time recording be organised in a 1–12 vehicle firm?

Options: forms, spreadsheet and software

In a one-vehicle firm, a paper form or freely structured records will do, as long as the details for every 24-hour period can be found. From two vehicles upwards, paper starts to leak: shifts, tachograph printouts and allowances payable are recorded in different places, and a missing entry at an inspection is your responsibility. Remember too that tachograph data must be kept for at least one year under Regulation (EU) No 165/2014. A spreadsheet is enough if you record with discipline, but it won't remind you of missing entries or total up overtime for you. At three vehicles a spreadsheet becomes prone to human error: one forgotten overtime entry a month per driver adds up to 36 entries a year, and they're missing at the inspection.

Selection criteria, and RAHTIS measured against them

Choose a tool that meets three conditions: it records start and finish times, calculates the overtime limits for you and passes data to the finance side without re-keying. In RAHTIS, job entries, driver shifts and documents are in the same place, which reduces the number of loose forms. To be honest, RAHTIS is not a comprehensive HR system covering Act 445/2019, nor does it replace tachograph data as the official source. When evaluating software, check three things: does it support the breakdown requirements of Finnish working time law, does it read tachograph file formats directly, and does it export to payroll? If all three are met, you'll save time every month.

Where RAHTIS doesn't help (yet)

Payroll export, annual leave records and automatic analysis of tachograph files are currently handled by other tools. RAHTIS's strength is managing jobs and transport, not serving as the final archive for statutory working time records. So combine RAHTIS entries with either a spreadsheet or a payroll program where the official records live. For example, you can export job details from RAHTIS as a CSV file and import them into your payroll program, where overtime and compensation are finally calculated. This two-system model is common in small firms, and it works as long as the transfer is documented and repeatable.

Step by step: a checklist for setting up statutory recording

Steps 1–7

  1. Establish whether your company is covered by the Finnish Drivers' Working Time Act (445/2019) or only by EU Working Time Directive 2002/15/EC – most 1–12 vehicle firms are covered by both.
  2. Decide how you will record: a spreadsheet, off-the-shelf working time software, or recording built into a system such as RAHTIS.
  3. Set the contractual working time for each driver and write it down.
  4. Introduce a recording template that captures working time, overtime, breaks and hours attracting pay supplements every day.
  5. Reconcile tachograph card data with the records at least once a week.
  6. Set the retention period to at least the two years required by law.
  7. Review the records every month and correct gaps straight away.

Monthly recurring routine

Block out a fixed slot in the calendar: check hours exceeding the limits, sign off any corrections with the drivers and back up the data. The same routine every month keeps you ready for inspection without a separate project. Also review the rest periods drivers actually took: was the 45-hour weekly rest taken, and did the 11-hour daily rest comply with the rules? If rest was reduced, check whether the reduction was permitted and whether compensating rest was given. Record these checks as part of the routine so you have evidence of regular monitoring if an inspector asks for it.

FAQ

Can a tachograph printout be used as working time records on its own?

No. Tachograph data covers driving, breaks and other work, but not shift start and finish times, periods of availability or information reported by the driver. Records only come into being when card data is combined with timesheets and job orders. Unclear periods, such as empty running or waiting at the loading point, must be marked separately so the inspector doesn't treat them as working time.

What do I do if a driver forgets to record overtime or breaks?

Correct the gaps straight away in the monthly routine by comparing the card hours with the records and signing off the corrections with the driver. Without an entry, the inspector will treat unclear periods as working time, which costs you in overtime pay or fines. Responsibility for the records always lies with the employer, so introduce a fixed weekly routine in which card data and records are reconciled before the month ends.

Do the working time rules also apply to owner-drivers and light goods transport?

The Finnish Act on the working and rest times of vehicle drivers (445/2019) applies to commercial road transport, so an owner-driver's own driving may also fall within its scope. For light goods transport and where the line for commercial operation lies, check the legislation itself. If your operations fall within the Act, the recording and retention obligations are the same as for employed drivers.

Do paper CMR consignment notes and tachograph charts have to be kept for the same length of time?

No. Tachograph charts and downloaded digital data must be kept for at least one year, but if the data is used as the basis for working time records, the two-year retention obligation applies to it too. Working time records must be kept for at least two years. Paper CMR consignment notes must be kept for at least five years under the international road transport convention, so they have the longest retention period of these three types of document.

Can I make a subcontractor responsible for recording working time?

Not entirely. Responsibility for recording lies with the employer, and a missing entry at an inspection is your responsibility, even if the recording is done externally. A subcontractor or software can do the practical work, but the obligations, such as two-year retention and inspection readiness, stay with you. That is why an outsourced service should be documented and the data it produces checked regularly.

kuorma-auton-kuljettajan-palkka.title: HGV driver pay in Finland
kuorma-auton-kuljettajan-palkka.description: HGV driver pay in Finland: the collective agreement pay table, experience increments and supplements explained, with a worked example of gross and net pay.
kuorma-auton-kuljettajan-palkka.html:
Key takeaways

  • An HGV driver in Finland typically earns around €3,000–3,800 a month before tax.
  • The collective agreement (TES) pay table sets the minimum wage, below which nothing can be agreed, and years of experience raise pay in steps.
  • Supplements, daily allowances and overtime pay can raise gross pay well above basic pay.
  • Posti follows its own collective agreement, so its pay levels can't be compared directly with other employers.
  • In the example, gross pay of €3,500 comes to roughly €2,700–2,850 net, and the employer's total cost is about €4,300.

An HGV driver's pay isn't a single figure but a sum: basic pay from the collective agreement (TES) pay table, an experience supplement, shift and overtime supplements, and taxable allowances. The collective agreement and the employer's own contract determine what a driver can earn, and Posti has its own table. This article unpicks the structure and works out an example of monthly net pay.

What is the average pay for an HGV driver in Finland?

An HGV driver in Finland typically earns around €3,000–3,800 a month before tax. The exact figure depends on experience, routes driven and supplements, but the baseline is set by the road transport collective agreement (TES), whose pay tables set drivers' minimum wages in full.

When you're pricing jobs or hiring a driver, the collective agreement table is the figure you can't go below. Everything above it is up to you: experience supplements, night and Sunday work, and per-kilometre or per-route payments quickly push the total up.

The same logic applies to earning from your own work. If you count trips, supplements and unpaid invoices by hand, any review of pay levels is only ever half done. RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/fi) keeps the voucher, consignment note and invoice in one chain, so you know what each shift actually brought in.

How is an HGV driver's pay set under the collective agreement?

An HGV driver's pay isn't at the employer's whim: the sector's generally binding collective agreement (TES) sets minimum wages, and no lower monthly wage may be agreed. If you run a firm with 1–12 vehicles, the pay table is the base to which you add experience pay, supplements and allowances.

What does the collective agreement pay table contain?

The pay table groups drivers by years of experience: the longer they've been in the trade, the higher the pay band they move up to. The table gives the minimum monthly wage, and alongside it there are experience-based pay rates, the principles of time-based and performance-based pay, and the terms of the employment contract. Below is an example of the structure; the figures are illustrative and do not replace the table currently in force:

Experience bandDescriptionMinimum wage (example)
Year 1No previous experience€2,400/month
Years 2–4Growing experience€2,550/month
Year 5 onwardsLong experience€2,700/month

Always take the exact figures from the collective agreement table currently in force, as they are updated with each agreement period. The table also covers separate provisions for drivers with a specialist vocational qualification and for transport using vehicle combinations over 12 tonnes. These factors raise the minimum wage automatically without separate negotiation.

How does the collective agreement bind the employer?

The collective agreement is binding: an employment contract may not set terms that are worse than the agreement, even if the driver agrees to them. The minimum wage is a floor, not a ceiling, so market pressure often pushes pay above it. If you employ drivers or are looking for work elsewhere, RAHTIS helps keep jobs and their profitability in order alongside pay: more information and the application form are at https://www.rahtis.eu/en/apply.

In practice, general applicability means that even an employer who isn't a member of the employers' federation has to comply with the terms of the collective agreement, provided the work done falls within the agreement's scope. You can check this on the website of SKAL (the Finnish Transport and Logistics association), which has up-to-date information on the agreements in force and their interpretation. If you don't want to risk disputes over interpretation, keep pay above the collective agreement table.

How much do experience and further training raise a driver's pay?

The collective agreement pay tables are built around years of experience: pay rises in steps as the driver's experience in the trade grows. In practice, a few years' experience moves a driver from the lower pay bands to the higher ones, and the effect shows directly in the hourly rate. According to the wage statistics of Statistics Finland, more experienced drivers' average earnings are clearly higher than the sector average (Statistics Finland wage statistics).

Additional certificates work in a different way. An ADR certificate for carrying dangerous goods, a qualification for operating loading equipment and add-on modules to a category C licence make a driver fit for work that would otherwise go unfilled. Many small operators pay extra for such work through the collective agreement supplements, so the certificate pays off for both driver and employer.

For an owner-driver, experience shows up through a different channel: as a seasoned professional you get more loads done and judge routes and return loads better. If you're planning to hire your first driver, put the experience requirement and additional certificates in the job advert and direct applicants to a detailed description of the work, for example via a freight platform.

Years of experience don't accrue automatically: the driver must be able to prove previous work history with payslips or employment certificates. The collective agreement also distinguishes between domestic and foreign experience, and experience driving abroad doesn't necessarily transfer directly into a pay band under the Finnish table. Bear this in mind if you're hiring experienced drivers from the Baltics or elsewhere abroad.

How much does Posti pay an HGV driver?

Posti follows its own collective agreement, which differs from the general road haulage collective agreement. In practice, this means a Posti driver's pay is set by Posti's own pay tables, and experience and area of work affect pay differently than for an ordinary haulier.

As a large employer, Posti also has its own supplement models: shift supplements, Sunday work enhancements and route-specific arrangements are part of its own agreement. So its pay doesn't tell you directly what you should pay your own driver.

When comparing pay, compare the whole package, not just basic pay. Work out your own pay level from your own collective agreement supplements and working hours, while making sure jobs and invoicing run without manual paperwork. RAHTIS helps keep track of who does what and who pays what, on our Latvian pages too (https://www.rahtis.eu/lv).

A particular feature of Posti's pay is the transparency and predictability of its supplements, whereas as a small operator you may have to negotiate each extra item separately. That can be an advantage when competing for staff, if you can offer a clear model in which the driver knows exactly what each route and shift will bring. A small operator's flexibility in agreeing terms can also work in your favour, as the pay structure can be tailored around that particular driver's strengths.

Which supplements and allowances make up an HGV driver's pay?

An HGV driver's pay isn't just the monthly salary: it includes supplements, daily allowances and mileage allowances, which can raise gross pay considerably. When you calculate a driver's pay yourself or compare costs when pricing a job, it's worth itemising these components separately.

How are supplements calculated?

Supplements are usually calculated as a percentage of basic pay or the hourly rate. Night work supplements, Sunday and public holiday supplements and overtime pay are set by the sector's collective agreement, and their size depends on when the work is done. The experience supplement and supplements for additional training also go into the same gross pay. In practice, this means two drivers on the same basic pay can receive different amounts each month if one of them drives nights and weekends.

The employer must keep records of all supplements and allowances so that they can be checked when the annual accounts are prepared and in any dispute over interpreting the collective agreement. Daily allowances paid for international driving must be itemised separately, because their tax treatment differs from ordinary pay. The Finnish Tax Administration records these allowances as a separate sum, and they must not be hidden in the general pay total.

What is paid on international work?

On international work, pay is topped up with a daily allowance, paid according to the number of hours for each day spent abroad, plus any supplements for cross-border work. Part of the daily allowance is tax-free, so it is a favourable component of pay in net terms. The collective agreement of Posti and its partners has its own provisions on drivers' supplements and allowances, which are worth checking directly in the collective agreement information published by Posti. When you invoice your own work or subcontracting, the RAHTIS API specifications help you feed job data and allowances straight into your invoicing system, so the paper "who owes what" notebook becomes unnecessary.

On international work, a driver may also receive a separate border-crossing allowance, paid for each border crossed. In practice this can mean tens of euros extra a week if the route passes through several countries. Parking charges and road tolls are not usually part of the driver's pay, but they must be included in the employer's total costs when pricing international haulage.

How does HGV driver pay vary by region and by employer?

The biggest pay differences don't come from regional boundaries but from the employer's size and contractual basis. At large operators such as Posti, the collective agreement pay scale is usually the base, with company-specific benefits added on top, whereas in small firms pay is often negotiated directly around the collective agreement minimum.

Regionally, pay in Uusimaa and Pirkanmaa is typically higher than in eastern and northern Finland, but the difference is often smaller than the difference in housing costs. Urban multi-drop and refuse collection work pays more than long-haul work, where overnight allowances make up part of the difference.

When looking at employers, check three things: does the company pay the collective agreement's general supplements in full, is overtime paid or does it go unpaid, and how regularly does the monthly pay include a performance-related element. The same driver doing the same work at two different companies can see a difference of several hundred euros in monthly pay.

Competition for drivers is fiercest in growth centres, where employers have to raise pay to keep up. An experienced driver can negotiate a better package at a small firm where the employer can't replace them quickly. Besides the Helsinki region, pay in port towns such as Kotka and Hamina is often above the local average, because export and import traffic constantly needs new drivers.

How does HGV driver pay compare with other jobs in transport?

In Finland, an HGV driver's pay is typically close to that of a bus driver or delivery driver, while taxi drivers and van drivers often earn less. The differences are largely explained by the collective agreements: on the HGV side, years of experience and further training raise pay predictably, whereas in lighter distribution pay is often hourly without the same experience ladder.

A maintenance worker or warehouse operative usually earns less than an experienced HGV driver, but office roles such as transport manager or invoicing specialist can exceed a driver's basic pay. The driver's advantage lies in supplements and allowances, which can lift total pay well above the basic hourly rate.

When comparing roles, always calculate net pay in the same way. The Finnish Tax Administration's salary calculator gives a comparable figure for different gross salaries: the Tax Administration salary calculator.

The comparison should also take account of the physical strain and irregular working hours typical of HGV driving. A delivery driver may get the same gross pay, but the work may be more physically demanding and involve more contact with customers. A long-haul driver, on the other hand, spends weeks away from home, which affects net pay once you take daily allowances and any other tax-free allowances into account. Comparing occupations is therefore multi-dimensional, and the monthly total alone doesn't tell the whole story.

Worked example: a driver's monthly gross and net pay

Take a hypothetical driver with five years' experience and basic haulage pay under the collective agreement table. Say the monthly salary is €3,200. On top of that comes performance pay, for example 300 kilometres per shift at €0.10, i.e. €30, plus 15 hours of overtime at the enhanced rate. Supplements and allowances bring gross pay to around €3,500.

Deducted from gross pay are the employee pension contribution (7.15% in 2025), the unemployment insurance contribution and tax according to the tax card. A rough rule of thumb: €3,500 gross comes to about €2,700–2,850 net, depending on the tax rate and deductions.

The cost to the employer is higher: pension contributions, health insurance and holiday pay add roughly 20–25% on top of gross pay, so a salary of €3,500 costs the employer about €4,300.

The calculation is indicative. The exact figures depend on the agreement's pay table, the amount of supplements and the driver's tax rate, so do your own calculation with your own figures before submitting a quote.

If the driver regularly works weekends, the Sunday supplement can raise monthly pay significantly. Under the collective agreement, Sunday work is paid at a 100% enhancement on top of the hourly rate, so a 10-hour Sunday shift adds about €150–200 gross, depending on the basic hourly rate. Similarly, the night work supplement, paid for hours between 22:00 and 06:00, can add 20–30%, which makes long night shifts a considerable boost to pay. When you're calculating pay for a quote, ask the driver how many weekend and night shifts they're prepared to do, so you can arrive at a realistic gross figure.

FAQ

Does an HGV driver have guaranteed pay if there is less work?

Yes, a monthly paid driver has guaranteed pay under the collective agreement, which is paid even when fewer jobs come in. The table's minimum wage is a floor below which pay cannot be agreed, even if the amount of work varies from week to week. Hourly paid arrangements follow different rules, so the type of employment contract is what decides.

How is a driver paid for overtime under the collective agreement?

Overtime is compensated with an enhancement under the collective agreement that increases with the number of overtime hours: a smaller supplement for the first hours, a larger one after that. The compensation is calculated by the hour and added to gross pay as taxable income. Monthly pay can rise noticeably if overtime builds up regularly: in the worked example, 15 hours of overtime raised gross pay.

Does the employer pay for a driver's Driver CPC training?

Initial and periodic Driver CPC training are usually paid for by the employer, since they are a prerequisite for the job. Additional certificates obtained by the driver, such as ADR or a loading equipment qualification, depend on the agreement. Many employers pay for them or compensate them through collective agreement supplements, because they make the driver more versatile.

Does pay rise if the driver also drives demanding vehicles or does ADR work?

Often, but not automatically. An ADR certificate and the ability to drive more demanding vehicles make the driver fit for work that would otherwise go unfilled, so market pressure and collective agreement supplements push pay up. Years of experience move the driver into higher pay bands, and extra allowances are usually paid separately for demanding runs.

kuormien-etsiminen-puheluiden-sijaan-rah.title: Finding loads on a freight exchange instead of by phone
kuormien-etsiminen-puheluiden-sijaan-rah.description: Find loads on a freight exchange instead of by phone: post your availability, search loads with filters and save hours of dispatch work every day.
kuormien-etsiminen-puheluiden-sijaan-rah.html:
Key takeaways

  • A freight exchange replaces phone calls: you post your availability and route, browse open loads and submit quotes with a single login.
  • Fill in your company details, vehicles, drivers' qualifications and payment terms in your profile before your first search.
  • On a platform, the job details, consignment note and payment tracking sit in the same view, so dispatch shifts from chasing information to making decisions.
  • The phone remains the fastest tool in urgent situations and with regular customers.
  • Check the other party's reliability through their business ID, company email address and the exchange's payment history data before accepting a job.

You can find loads on a freight exchange instead of by phone: you upload your availability and route to the platform, browse open loads along your route and bid for them with a single login. This guide compares a day on the phone with a day on the platform side by side, and gives you checklists for the profile, availability and route settings worth sorting out before your first search.

Why does finding loads by phone still take hours?

When you're the dispatcher, the bookkeeper and the drivers' boss all at once, searching by phone eats the hours: you ring brokers one by one, listen to prices, jot jobs down on a scrap of paper and hope someone rings back. The same empty leg you could fill in ten minutes takes half a day.

The hidden costs of phone-based searching in a 1–12 lorry firm

The hidden costs aren't the per-minute call charges but the interrupted work: every call breaks off invoicing, checking CMR notes or planning the next job. The note on a scrap of paper saying "who pays and when" gets forgotten precisely when you need the money most.

In a three-lorry business, a single dispatch run can mean 15–20 calls a day just to fill empty legs. Each call lasts three to five minutes on average, but the real cost is the context switch: when you go back to invoicing after a call, it takes fifteen minutes to get back up to speed. Ten calls a day in practice means an hour and a half of fragmented working time that vanishes from the diary without anyone noticing.

In a one-person business it's worse: when you're driving yourself and making calls during breaks, searching by phone eats into driving time. A break that should be a rest turns into a stressful round of calls with uncertain results. Voicemail is the most common answer, and leaving a call-back request means waiting around, which only adds to fatigue.

Freight exchanges are built for exactly this: Teleroute describes how its service works as shippers publishing loads and hauliers finding them using search criteria, with no phone call (Teleroute). RAHTIS starts from the same problem at the smaller end: you publish the job once and follow it step by step (RAHTIS – Veokorraldus ja veobörs).

How does a freight exchange find a load for your lorry?

A freight exchange works as a two-way marketplace: shippers publish loads, and hauliers find them with filters or by posting their own empty legs. The system matches the two sides automatically when the details fit. The same logic applies in RAHTIS (RAHTIS – Transportledning och lastbörs): a published load is visible to those searching, and you follow the job step by step.

Search filters: origin, destination, date and vehicle type

The search is based on four fields. Origin and destination define your route, the date tells when the lorry is free, and the vehicle type (refrigerated, trailer, container chassis) weeds out loads your vehicle isn't suited to. The more precisely these are filled in on your profile, the fewer matches you get that you have to turn down.

In practice the chain of filters works like this: first you choose the origin area, for example "Helsinki + 150 km". Then you add a destination filter, such as "Tampere or Turku". The third filter is the date: "loading Monday morning, delivery Tuesday". The fourth is the vehicle type: "drop trailer, 13.6 metres, tail lift". The system only shows the loads that pass all four filters. If you leave one field empty, you get dozens of matches that don't suit your vehicle, and you waste time scrolling through them.

Posting an offer vs searching actively

In an active search you browse the loads on offer yourself and submit quotes. By posting your empty leg, you tell the other side where you're heading and when, and the load can come to you. In practice the two complement each other: searching fills the lorry today, and a posted empty leg finds the return load for tomorrow.

What information do you need to prepare before you start searching for loads online?

An exchange search only works first time if your profile, vehicle details and route settings are in order before you open your first request for quotation. An incomplete profile shows up as a bidder nobody picks.

Profile checklist

  • Company details: business ID (Y-tunnus), VAT number, insurance and CMR liability details
  • Vehicles: lorries, trailers, payload, lifting equipment, number of lashing straps
  • Drivers: licence categories, ADR qualification, languages spoken
  • Payment terms and invoicing details ready in advance, so they aren't up for negotiation on every job

Many exchanges show the other party's credit rating and reviews before you quote. Trans.eu's documentation covers, among other things, members' ratings and payment history (Trans.eu Help Center). It's worth gathering the same information about your own customers: in RAHTIS (RAHTIS – Kuljetusten hallinta ja rahtipörssi) you can track not only the job status but also who pays what.

Availability and route settings checklist

SettingWhat to prepare
Origin areasHome town + 100–200 km radius
Empty-leg daysCalendar for the next 2 weeks
Route preferencesAreas to avoid, your preferred routes
Return load conditionsMinimum rate, maximum length, unloading time
Vehicle availabilityFree lorry + trailer, loading time
Pricing guidelinesMinimum rate per km, separate surcharges

Once these are filled in, a quote is a click, not a phone call.

A day on the phone vs a day on the platform: the dispatch workflow side by side

Morning: finding loads and quoting

On a phone day, the morning goes on calls: nobody can see who has a spot load available, so the enquiries go one after another. On a platform day, you open the freight exchange, filter routes and loading times, and see the available loads at a glance. Submitting a quote takes a couple of clicks, and replies arrive as notifications without the phone ringing while you're driving.

Daytime: confirmations, consignment note, driver details

This is where the difference is greatest. In the phone model, the booking, load details and consignment note files live in different places: text messages, email and a scrap of paper. On a platform, the same job appears as a single whole: the driver sees the addresses, times and consignment note directly on their phone, and you follow the status without ringing to ask "where are you?".

When loads, drivers and documents are in the same system, dispatch shifts from chasing information to making decisions: you choose the next load, and the system passes the information on. In RAHTIS, the consignment note, confirmation and status tracking sit in the same view, so in a four-lorry business you no longer leaf through scraps of paper to see who pays and what's still open. The same principle works for a small Nordic business whichever exchange its spot loads come from, and the Latvian-language RAHTIS page (RAHTIS – Transporta vadība un kravu birža) explains how to bring your own customers and exchange jobs together. An honest note: if there aren't enough loads on the platform for a particular route, you'll still have to make calls or check another exchange, so the phone won't disappear entirely.

Evening: invoicing and payment tracking

On a phone day, the evening goes on matching consignment notes with quote notes to raise invoices. On a platform, the end of a job prompts for the POD, and the invoice goes out from the same chain. Payment tracking is visible in the system, so you no longer need a "who owes what" list in a paper notebook.

What are the risks of giving up the phone, and how do you vet the other party?

A phone call is the traditional way to "sniff out" whether a client is reliable, but systematic checks can replace it: online, a fraudster leaves a trail, as long as you note the details down before accepting the job.

Counterparty checklist

Before accepting a load from a freight exchange, check at least: the company's official name and business ID, the client's contact details on a company email address (not a Gmail address), payment history from the exchange's rating points, and whether the client is a verified member. Trans.eu and TIMOCOM both offer members' credit ratings and payment behaviour data for exactly this purpose (Trans.eu credit information service). Keep the list and fill it in for every new client, even if the load is urgent.

Payment terms and advance payments

The biggest risk isn't a wrong address but money: is payment at 30 days or 60, and who pays if the goods arrive but the invoice isn't paid? Agree payment terms in writing before loading, and beware of cash-in-advance requests, which are a common scam. In RAHTIS, the job details, consignment note and invoicing run through the same step-by-step view, so the agreement and documents stay paired (RAHTIS – Transportmanagement und Frachtenbörse).

When is the phone still the better option, even if you use a freight exchange?

The phone beats the platform when time is short. If the lorry is standing empty and a spot load has to be found within the hour, a direct call to a shipper you know or to other hauliers working the area is often the fastest way to get a load moving.

The second situation is an urgent or unusual load. If the loading changes mid-day, a trailer is missing or the delivery time falls through, it's sorted on the phone in seconds. Writing a message and waiting for a reply takes the same minutes.

The third reason is relationships. Your regular customers and most important clients are used to hearing from you, and direct contact maintains trust when spot loads from the freight exchange alone aren't enough to fill the week.

So in practice: the exchange handles searching and paperwork, the phone handles urgency and relationships.

How do you start searching for loads digitally when you have no history on the platform yet?

A new account is a blank sheet, but the first job comes sooner if your profile doesn't look anonymous. Fill in your company details, registration numbers, number of drivers and insurance details straight away, and upload a sample CMR or two from previous deliveries. Respond to your first quotes within a few minutes: on platforms, response time is visible to the other side, and a quick acknowledgement makes up for a missing review history.

Start with small spot loads in your local area, even if the margin is thin. The first successful jobs earn the reviews that open up better-paid routes. Be as careful as you would on the phone: confirm the loading time in writing, ask for a signed consignment note and send the POD straight away.

In small hauliers' experience, it's precisely this combination, load search, POD and invoicing in the same workflow, that makes the switch worthwhile once the paper notebook and separate logins start to become a burden (Reddit discussion of a small haulier's TMS experience).

Which tools for a small haulage business: exchanges and TMS in one package?

For a small business, tools fall into two camps: freight exchanges such as Trans.eu, TIMOCOM, Teleroute, Transportial and Maxmove handle finding loads and filling spot capacity, while a TMS handles dispatch, consignment notes and invoicing. Many run them side by side: the exchange login in one window, a scrap of paper in another, email in a third.

What RAHTIS is suited to and where it falls short

RAHTIS combines both: the shipper publishes the job once and follows the work step by step, while the haulier fills empty legs and keeps the whole fleet in one place. It works from a single lorry upwards, so exchange logins, the notebook and paper CMRs are replaced by a workflow found in a single view.

To be honest, RAHTIS doesn't solve everything. It doesn't replace accounting software or a bank connection, and it doesn't know the loads on every foreign exchange. If you need a wide international load supply or advanced reporting for a larger fleet, a traditional exchange and a bigger TMS may suit you better. RAHTIS is designed for one to twelve lorries.

FAQ

Is using a freight exchange chargeable for a small firm, and how does pricing usually work?

Most exchanges charge a monthly or annual subscription that varies with membership size and features. Some charge separately for each confirmed job. Compare pricing based on your own volumes: for one to three lorries a lighter subscription is often enough, and trial periods help you test whether searching pays off before you commit.

Can I combine several exchanges (e.g. Teleroute, TIMOCOM, Trans.eu) into one search without separate logins?

Usually not directly: the exchanges are separate systems, each with its own login and its own filters. In practice, small hauliers keep one or two exchanges open side by side or use a separate TMS that brings jobs together in one view. RAHTIS meets this need by gathering your own jobs and exchange work under the same workflow.

How is the CMR consignment note handled when the load comes through an exchange?

The consignment note details come with the job information, but signing still takes place at the loading and delivery points. In digital workflows, the driver fills in and signs the CMR on a phone and sends the POD to the system immediately after delivery. A paper version is still an acceptable backup. The most important thing is that the consignment note and the other job details stay in the same chain.

How quickly are loads usually found once a listing is published on the platform?

On popular routes with standard vehicles, offers start coming in within hours, sometimes minutes. With a less common vehicle type or in a remote area, a listing may go days without a match. The quality of the listing directly affects the result: precise availability times, route and vehicle details produce matches faster than a vague listing nobody dares take on.

Do I need a separate TMS, or is a freight exchange account enough?

It depends on how much other work falls outside the exchange. An exchange account handles finding loads, but dispatch, consignment notes, payment tracking and invoicing remain separate tasks. If you run one to twelve lorries and want jobs, documents and invoicing in one view, a TMS adds value. For occasional work with a single lorry, an exchange account may be enough to start with.

miten-laatia-rahtitarjous-nopeasti-asiak.title: How to put together a haulage quote for a customer quickly
miten-laatia-rahtitarjous-nopeasti-asiak.description: Build a haulage quote in minutes from seven fields: route, load, vehicle, price, validity, payment terms and contact details. Send it while still on the call.
miten-laatia-rahtitarjous-nopeasti-asiak.html:
Key takeaways

  • Build your haulage quote from seven fields: company details, route, load details, vehicle type, price with justification, validity period and payment terms.
  • Unless a return load is confirmed, price in empty running using the kilometres for both directions, and tell the customer so plainly.
  • Always state the validity period, for example seven days; otherwise the quote stays open forever and the price of fuel may change.
  • Justify the price with the route, vehicle type and schedule rather than discounts, and most price haggling stops of its own accord.
  • A freight exchange gives you ready-made load details and a market rate to which you add your own margin; RAHTIS keeps the quote, the CMR and the invoice in one workflow.

Put together a haulage quote in minutes by filling in seven fields: company details, route, vehicle type, price and its justification, validity period, payment terms and contact details. With the structure ready as a template, the quote goes to the customer while you are still on the phone, not a day later after being scribbled in a notebook. This guide shows how to do it in practice, field by field. If you want a broader overview of transport management and the freight exchange, take a look at RAHTIS – Transport management and freight exchange: loose trailers, containers and express deliveries.

How do you put together a haulage quote for a customer quickly?

In five minutes, if the information is to hand and you know the structure by heart: origin and destination, type of load, weight and volume, schedule, price and payment terms. Write these seven lines in the same order every time and the quote takes shape during the call rather than afterwards in a notebook.

To calculate the price, use the basis for calculating haulage rates and cost recovery published by SKAL (the Finnish Transport and Logistics association), which hauliers in Finland rely on. Once the basis is clear, the quote can be justified straight away. In RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/fi) the same information pre-fills the quote form.

Speed comes from repetition. If you always use the same template, nobody needs to do creative writing in the middle of a busy call. Start the call by asking about the route and the load, after which the price is the only open variable. Enter the answers straight into the ready-made fields and send the message as soon as the call ends.

What information must a haulage quote contain?

Company details and the customer

Start the quote with your company details: name, Business ID, address and a contact person with phone number. Do the same for the customer, so that the documents later match the consignment note and the invoice. Without a Business ID the customer cannot check who they are handing their load to.

A missing Business ID causes invoicing delays and possible mix-ups if there are several companies with the same name. Make sure the contact person is the one who actually makes the decisions, not someone who just passes messages on. This shortens the approval process considerably.

Route, vehicle type and load details

This is the heart of the quote. Write down the details that determine the price and prevent misunderstandings about the load:

FieldExampleWhy it matters
Origin and destinationVantaa → TampereDistance determines the price and the empty running
Load8 Euro pallets, 6,000 kgDetermines the vehicle type
Vehicle typeSemi-trailer, drawbar trailer, tankerWrong type = cancellation
ScheduleCollection Thursday 8–12, delivery FridayUrgency costs extra
Additional servicesUnloading, loading, temperature monitoringA hidden cost if forgotten

If the load needs a specialist vehicle or ADR certification, say so plainly in the quote. Fewer questions later.

Giving the load dimensions in metres and kilograms is more precise than a pallet count alone. For example, "8 pallets, 120×80×200 cm, 6,000 kg in total" gives the driver confidence that the load will fit and stay within the weight limits. If you leave out the dimensions, the customer may assume standard-size pallets when the load is in fact out of gauge.

Validity period and payment terms

Without a validity period the quote stays open forever, and the price of fuel may change before the customer replies. State, for example, "valid for 7 days", or tie the price to a specific departure date. Payment terms belong in the quote from the start: 14 days net is common, and if you need 30 days, agree it before the job is done. The RAHTIS API documentation (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/api-docs) shows how these fields carry over from the quote to the consignment note and the invoice without retyping.

The validity period protects you against swings in market prices, especially fuel. If you tie the price to a specific departure date, the customer understands that delays may lead to a new quote. Stating the payment terms in the quote prevents surprises at invoicing and gives the customer a chance to comment on the terms before the job starts.

How do you price a haulage job in minutes?

Fixed price or hourly rate

Choose the model according to the nature of the job. A fixed price suits regular runs where the route and the type of work are known in advance. An hourly rate makes sense when the work includes unloading, waiting or several drops that you cannot estimate beforehand.

The advantage of a fixed price is predictability for the customer: they know the exact sum in advance and need not fear unexpected costs. The advantage of an hourly rate is on your side: if unloading drags on or the customer is late, you invoice for the work done. Many hauliers use a hybrid: a fixed price for the basic job and an hourly rate for extra work, such as waiting beyond the agreed time.

Empty running and return loads

Let us work through an example you can apply directly to your own jobs. Start from a rate per kilometre that covers fuel, the driver's wages, insurance and vehicle wear, and add your margin. If the customer's job is 300 km but there is no confirmed return load for the journey home, price it on 600 kilometres, i.e. both directions. This is fair, because an empty kilometre costs you almost as much as a loaded one.

Tell the customer plainly that the price includes the empty leg; that way the justification is ready and neither side has to guess. If you get a return load from the freight exchange or from your own customers, you can take the empty running out and offer a more competitive price. In RAHTIS you publish your empty legs at https://www.rahtis.eu/et/apply, so a return load can cover part of the journey before the quote goes out.

A concrete example: the rate is €1.20 per kilometre and the margin is 15 per cent. A one-way 300 km job with no return load costs 600 km × €1.20 × 1.15 = €828. If you find a return load, the price drops to 300 km × €1.20 × 1.15 = €414. That €414 difference is your room to negotiate while still keeping your margin.

Which extra costs to include

Include a waiting time agreement (e.g. first hour free, hourly rate after that), quality-related charges, weather delays and handling of the CMR consignment note. Traficom (the Finnish Transport and Communications Agency) provides guidance on consignment note and CMR requirements in road transport (Traficom), so make sure your extra charges also cover the documentation, whether electronic or on paper.

Forgetting extra costs is the most common reason a profitable job turns into a loss-maker. For example, occasional waiting at the delivery point can stretch to hours, and if you have not agreed compensation, you are doing it in your own time. Always state the waiting terms in the quote: the first hour is included in the price, after that €45–60 per hour.

How do you justify the price to the customer without haggling?

A good quote justifies the price with the route, vehicle type and schedule, not with discounts. When the quote shows the kilometres, the nature of the route (for example a loose trailer with no return load), the type of vehicle needed and the collection and delivery times, the customer can see where the money goes. Empty running and the lack of a return route are real costs, and showing them openly stops most price haggling.

Also state what is included: the consignment note (CMR), waiting time terms and payment terms. When everything is in writing, the negotiation moves from details to the overall price, which you have already justified.

The same principle works for your own customers and for jobs from the freight exchange. Once a quote has been built properly, the next one goes out as a copy. In RAHTIS you can build a reusable quote template for your own routes and sign up at https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/apply, from a single lorry upwards.

Justification matters even more when you are competing with larger operators. Big companies can offer a low rate per kilometre, but they carry overheads and delays. Your advantage is speed and flexibility. When you base the price realistically on costs and show the calculation openly, a small haulier can win a tender against a bigger operator, because the customer understands how the price is made up and trusts it.

How do you send the quote and follow up the reply?

Email works for regular customers, but the message easily gets lost in the customer's inbox. Freight exchange messaging is the fastest way to reach those looking for a loose trailer move: Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu, for example, handle the quote and the reply in the same system, so you have a written record of the price and terms (how a freight exchange works).

Choose the channel to suit the job: email for a regular customer, the freight exchange for an empty leg, RAHTIS when you want everything in one place. In RAHTIS you publish the job once, carriers reply directly and the transport progresses step by step in the same view: https://www.rahtis.eu/lt/apply.

Follow-up is the part that a notebook-and-spreadsheet setup loses. Set a reminder for 24 hours later: if there is no reply, call or send a follow-up message. Log every quote you send and its status (pending, rejected, accepted), so you can see each week which customers and which routes actually pay.

Following up quotes is a numbers game. If you send ten quotes a week and three are left hanging without a reply, you are losing potential turnover. A simple spreadsheet with columns for customer, route, price, date sent and status is enough to get started. When you see, for example, that 80 per cent of your quotes on the Helsinki–Turku route are accepted, you can focus more on it.

How does a freight exchange speed up the quoting process?

What freight exchanges offer for quoting

A freight exchange gives you ready-made load details that you would otherwise collect by phone and write in a notebook: origin and destination, date, trailer type, weight and load description. When a customer asks for a quote, you check the rate for a comparable route on the exchange and add your own margin on top. Transportial, Teleroute, TIMOCOM, Trans.eu and Maxmove all work on the same principle here: they show the market rate on the route, and you decide whether to go below or above it.

The exchange also shortens negotiation. When the customer sees that there is demand on the route, your price is easier to accept without a long tussle.

Seeing the market rate gives you a realistic idea of the prices other operators are working at. If your own price is clearly above the market, you can either lower it or justify the difference: faster delivery, fewer delays or better customer service. If your price is below the market, you can raise your margin without losing the customer.

RAHTIS on routes and empty legs

In RAHTIS the whole chain is in one place: you publish a load or a loose trailer once, see empty legs and return journeys on your own route, and quote directly on the basis of the same information. Once the job is accepted, it carries on as a transport, a consignment note and an invoice without you moving data between the exchange, a spreadsheet and a notebook.

An honest limitation: RAHTIS is not yet as large an international marketplace as the established exchanges, so for finding loose trailer moves abroad you may need another exchange alongside it.

How does RAHTIS handle the quote and the transport in one place?

RAHTIS brings together the same steps that a haulier with 4 lorries described on Reddit: separate freight exchange logins, an outdated TMS and a paper notebook of who owes what (Reddit thread on a small haulier's working day). In RAHTIS you write the quote once, the customer accepts it and the same job carries on through the workflow without copy-pasting.

While the job is under way, the driver and the shipper follow its status step by step, the consignment note (CMR) is created in the system and, once the POD is received, the invoice goes out from the same place. You do not need to move data separately from a quote spreadsheet to invoicing software and a notebook.

To be honest, RAHTIS does not replace everything: it is not a freight exchange in the same sense as Trans.eu or Teleroute, where you browse an open marketplace for loose trailer moves, and it does not have the range of enterprise add-ons that McLeod or Turvo offer. RAHTIS is designed for small operators, from a single lorry upwards, and its strength is precisely that the quote, the transport and the invoice live in the same workflow instead of in three different programs.

Joining up the workflow saves time, but even more important is the reduction in errors. When you move data by hand from the quote to the consignment note and from there to the invoice, every transfer is a chance to type the wrong address, weight or price. In a single system the data stays unchanged from start to finish, and the customer receives the correct invoice at the correct address.

What are the most common mistakes in a haulage quote and how do you avoid them?

The first mistake is a missing validity period. Without a date the quote lives forever, and the customer may come back three weeks later demanding the same price even though fuel prices have changed. Always add a line saying "quote valid for 7 days" or similar.

The second mistake is a vague vehicle type. "Lorry" does not tell anyone whether the job suits a drawbar trailer, a swap body or a van. If the customer assumes something else and you send the wrong vehicle, the empty running is at your expense. State the type, volume and payload.

The third mistake is forgetting the payment terms. An agreement noted in a paper notebook without terms means that "who owes what" is left to your memory. State the payment period, for example 14 days net, and whether you charge interest on late payment.

These three lines take a minute but save negotiation and debt-chasing later.

The fourth mistake is missing detail in the load description. "Pallets" is not enough, as pallets can come in different sizes and contain different goods. State the number of pallets, the dimensions and the weight, so the driver knows what they are collecting and what space the load will fit in. The fifth mistake is forgetting additional services: if the customer expects unloading and you have priced only the transport, the job becomes a loss-maker.

FAQ

Can I send a haulage quote directly to a freight exchange without a customer of my own?

Yes, you can. Freight exchanges such as Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu list loose trailer jobs that you can respond to directly in the system without an existing customer relationship. The exchange gives you the details ready-made: route, date, vehicle type, weight and load description. You add your own margin and submit the quote. This works particularly well for filling empty legs.

What should I do if the customer asks for a discount on the quote?

If the quote justifies the price with the route, vehicle type, kilometres and schedule, most price haggling stops of its own accord. When the customer sees where the money goes, the negotiation moves to the overall price. If a discount is still requested, see whether a return load is available: it lets you take out the empty running, making the price genuinely more competitive without the deal becoming a loss.

How long is a haulage quote valid by default?

There should be no default: always state the validity period, for example seven days. Without a date the quote remains open forever, and the customer may come back weeks later demanding the same price even though fuel has gone up. Alternatively, you can tie the price to a specific departure date, so the schedule sets the validity for you.

Do I need a separate TMS if I only send a few quotes a week?

Not necessarily. A notebook and a spreadsheet work until the quote, the consignment note and the invoice live in different places and the data has to be moved by hand. For a small haulier, from a single lorry upwards, RAHTIS handles the quote, the transport, the CMR and the invoice in one workflow without copy-pasting. Once the quote template has been built, the next quote goes out as a copy in minutes.

miten-loittaa-palautuskuorma-tyhjelle-au.title: How to find a return load for an empty lorry
miten-loittaa-palautuskuorma-tyhjelle-au.description: How to find a return load for an empty lorry: channels in order of priority, a margin decision tree and a routine that replaces hit-and-miss load hunting.
miten-loittaa-palautuskuorma-tyhjelle-au.html:
Key takeaways

  • Look for a return load in a fixed order: your own customers first, then freight exchanges along the route, and terminals and ports last.
  • Compare every load with the cost of running empty: the freight rate minus fuel, tolls and extra working hours decides whether the load is worth taking.
  • Before quoting, check four points: route, timing, equipment and payment terms; if one fails, running home empty is often the cheaper option.
  • Write your offer precisely: equipment, available time, route, price and driver details, so the shipper replies to you.
  • Check the payment period and the payment default register before committing, as late payment interest and the right to recovery costs are based on the Finnish Interest Act.

Check your channels in a fixed order: your own customers first, then freight exchanges along your route, then other hauliers in the same area. Assess each load with a decision tree: route, timing, equipment and payment terms. This article gives you both in concrete terms, plus a routine that replaces hit-and-miss hunting.

What is a return load and why is an empty lorry a cost risk?

A return load, or backhaul, is freight you take on for the journey home when your own customer's job or a freight exchange job ends in the wrong place. Empty running (a trailer with no load) means the same journey with no income. Freight exchanges such as Trans.eu and Teleroute list these return loads all the time, and RAHTIS matches the empty legs of your own fleet directly with jobs on offer (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi).

Empty running is not just fuel: it is lost margin

An empty lorry has the same cost structure as a loaded one: fuel, the driver's wages, insurance, tyres and depreciation all run, but no money comes in. In European road haulage roughly a fifth of vehicle-kilometres are driven empty, which is capacity wasted outright (Eurostat, Road freight transport statistics).

When you run 300 kilometres empty, you do not just lose fuel. You lose the amount the return load would have brought in, less fuel and tolls. That is why looking for return loads should be a routine, not hit-and-miss hunting.

Which channels should you search for return loads first, and in what order?

It pays to dig for return loads in a set order: your own customers first, then regular partners, then freight exchanges and terminals last. The order is based on where you get the best price and the least risk relative to the time spent searching.

1. Your own customers and regular partners

Call or message the customers and subcontracting partners whose routes cross the route of your empty lorry. You already know how they pay and what equipment they need, so the negotiation takes a minute. Ask in particular about regular loads on set weekdays: one fixed return load a week is worth more than a one-off load.

2. Freight exchanges and load boards

If your own network turns up nothing, open the freight exchanges. Those used in Finland and Northern Europe include Teleroute, TIMOCOM, Trans.eu and Maxmove; an option that combines transport planning and load search is RAHTIS (https://www.rahtis.eu/sv). The biggest difference between the channels is how quickly you see new loads along your route.

ChannelSearch based onMain benefitsDrawbacks
Own customersPhone and emailPrice, reliable payment termsLimited volume, relies on memory
Freight exchangeRoute and equipment searchLarge number of loads, speedPrice competition, unknown counterparty
TerminalOn site or by phoneLoose trailer and port loads close byUncertain schedules, tight pricing

3. Terminals, ports and loose trailer traffic

Last of all, check the terminals and ports along the route: loose trailer and container loads often only appear on the day. These carry the highest risk, because waiting times and payment terms vary, so take them only when the other channels have come up empty.

How do route and timing affect which loads are worth offering to carry?

The direction of the route, when loads are posted and how flexible the load is decide which return loads are realistically available. The same lorry gets different results on a different day and on a different corridor.

Route direction and the rhythm of port traffic

Empty running is most likely in the direction where the least freight moves. Loose trailers leaving ports and industrial hubs head inland on weekday mornings, so an empty lorry at a port in the afternoon is competing for very few loads. The opposite direction, from rural areas to the hubs, often offers more jobs but lower rates. Equipment narrows the choice: a reefer load will not be offered to a flatbed, and a required loading time rules out long repositioning runs.

Timing: when loads are posted and when they disappear

Freight exchanges such as Teleroute and TIMOCOM post loads around the clock, but in practice new offers tend to appear in the mornings and afternoons, and urgent ones are gone within hours. If your lorry will be empty at 12 noon tomorrow, offer to take loads whose collection time is flexible, and keep your phone free for the morning posting window. Jobs published in RAHTIS are visible step by step, so you can follow the shipper's schedule changes without calling; the terms of use set out which party notifies cancellations and when (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/kayttoehdot). Speed of response often matters more than price.

How do you decide whether to take a return load or run home empty?

An empty journey home always costs money: fuel, time and wear accumulate even though there is no income. A return load is almost always worth taking if it covers the variable costs and leaves even a small margin. The sum is simple: the freight rate offered minus fuel, tolls and extra working hours. If what is left is more than the cost of running empty, the load wins.

Decision tree: four questions before you quote

Before quoting, go through four points in this order. The first is the route: does the load take you towards your next job or your home base, or do you have to go 200 km out of your way, making the actual journey longer? The second is timing: can loading and unloading be done before the job you have already agreed, and is there enough buffer for delays? The third is equipment: do the trailer type, lifting gear or heating meet the load's requirements, or would you need extra kit you do not otherwise carry? The fourth is payment terms: ask about the payment period straight away, and if it is 60 days or more, price the delay in or do not quote. If any of the four fails, running home empty is often cheaper than taking a bad load.

Checklist: equipment, weight, time, payment terms

Before quoting, check: the total weight and floor area of the load against your own equipment, the loading and unloading times (unpaid hours can easily eat the margin), tolls and ferry fares on the route, and the consignment note and CMR details in advance. Also bear in mind the risk that there will be no next load ready at the delivery point.

All in all, the decision is the same every time: work out the margin, compare it with the cost of running empty and decide within five minutes. RAHTIS shows the route, timing and payment terms of a job in the same view, so comparing is quicker than leafing through a notebook and separate exchange logins (https://www.rahtis.eu/et). The system does not make the decision for you, but it removes the searching, which is often the reason bad loads are taken in a rush.

What should you put in a load offer to get a reply?

An offer that gets a reply contains five points: equipment (e.g. crane or refrigerated trailer, payload), availability window in hours, route from collection to delivery and return, price and driver details. Write the price clearly: is it fixed or negotiable, and does it include waiting time?

Add one line that makes the biggest difference: "Available [date, time] on [town]–[town], equipment [specify], price [€]." A vague "we have space" is ignored, because the shipper is comparing dozens of offers within minutes.

Driver details and liability issues are best agreed in writing at the offer stage, since the entries in the consignment note bind the carrier under the liability rules of the CMR Convention (CMR material from the Finnish transport and logistics sector). In RAHTIS the offer and the job details travel in the same system, so no paper is needed; the features are listed in more detail in the product description.

How do you avoid the payment and liability risks of return loads?

A return load from a freight exchange often comes from an unknown shipper, so check their ability to pay before you commit. Ask directly about the payment period and, if necessary, ask for payment in advance on the first job. In Finland, late payment interest and the right to recovery costs are laid down in the Interest Act (korkolaki) (Finlex, Interest Act), so collecting overdue freight charges is not merely a matter for negotiation. Keep a record of each customer's payment times so you notice who repeatedly pays late.

Payment terms and credit information

The Finnish Trade Register shows that a company exists, but payment default information should be checked separately in a payment default register before a larger job. A security deposit or a trading account rating on the exchange (e.g. Trans.eu or TIMOCOM) gives an indication of how the shipper pays, but it does not replace your own judgement. Running home empty is sometimes cheaper than freight paid 60 days late.

CMR and liability for the load

Fill in the CMR consignment note carefully: the quantity as counted at dispatch and any remarks on the apparent condition of the goods protect you in the event of damage. Under the CMR Convention, the exemptions available to the carrier limit your liability, but exceptions (e.g. an incorrect description by the shipper) should be recorded on the document itself. A paper notebook is not enough as evidence if a dispute arises only weeks later.

How do you turn finding return loads into a regular routine rather than hit-and-miss hunting?

Hit-and-miss hunting means you open the exchange only when the lorry is already empty and the phone is ringing. A routine means that fleet status, alerts and the order of work are ready before you need them. Three steps are enough.

Recording fleet status in advance

Every morning, write down which lorry is where, where it is heading back to, when it will be free and what equipment it has (trailer, crane, temperature requirement). This takes five minutes and is the foundation of the whole routine, because without it you do not know what return load you are actually looking for. A paper notebook will do, but it is worth having the same information on your phone as well.

Alerts and filters on the exchange

Do not browse the freight exchange by hand. Set filters for your usual routes: origin, destination direction, date and equipment requirement, and switch on alerts for new postings. When an offer comes in, reply quickly with a complete offer whose structure is already ready from previous jobs.

One tool instead of several exchanges

Several separate exchange and TMS logins are exactly the mess that eats up a one-person planner's day. In RAHTIS you publish a job once, follow it step by step and handle consignment notes and invoicing in the same place. To be honest, RAHTIS does not yet bring all external freight exchanges together in one view the way larger systems do, so some of the exchange checking remains your responsibility. The routine stays the same though: record your fleet, let the alerts do the work for you and reply quickly.

FAQ

The return load does not cover the whole journey – is it still worth taking?

Often, yes. Work out the margin for the whole journey: the freight rate offered minus fuel, tolls and extra working hours, and compare the result with the cost of the empty kilometres. If a part-journey load covers the variable costs and leaves even a small margin, it beats running empty. The exception is a detour that lengthens the overall journey too much.

How long before an empty run should you start looking for a return load?

As soon as you know when the lorry will be free and what the return route is, which is often a day or two before the empty run. Loads appear on the exchanges in the mornings and afternoons, and urgent ones are gone within hours. Set up filters and alerts in advance so that you see new loads straight away without constant browsing.

Can a return load be priced lower than normal freight, and how do I justify the price?

Yes, it can, because the lorry is heading back anyway. Justify the offer by the fact that the load fits a route and time already planned: collection and delivery fit the agreed times, the equipment is the right type and there is no extra mileage. State the price precisely and say whether waiting time is included, so that the shipper can compare easily.

What do I do if the shipper of a return load does not pay?

Ask about the payment period at the offer stage and keep a record of customers' payment times. In Finland, late payment interest on overdue freight charges and the right to recovery costs are based on the Interest Act, so collection is not merely a matter for negotiation. For larger jobs, check the payment default register in advance; if the payment period is 60 days or more, price the delay in or do not quote.

Do I need a separate contract or a CMR for a return load taken from an exchange?

A CMR consignment note is always needed, and it should be filled in carefully: the quantity as counted at dispatch and any remarks on the apparent condition of the goods protect you if there is damage. Driver details and liability issues are best agreed in writing at the offer stage, since the liability rules of the CMR Convention are binding. Each exchange's terms of use supplement the contract but do not replace the entries in the consignment note.

odotusajan-kirjaus-satulastauksessa-kulj.title: Recording waiting time during trailer swaps: a guide for drivers
odotusajan-kirjaus-satulastauksessa-kulj.description: Recording waiting time during trailer swaps: required fields, sample entries and tips to make the record stand up to payroll checks and inspection.
odotusajan-kirjaus-satulastauksessa-kulj.html:
Key takeaways

  • Waiting time during a trailer swap is working time when the driver is on a task assigned by the employer and has been instructed to be there.
  • An accepted entry includes the start and end time, the location, the type of task and a reference such as the consignment note number.
  • The most common reasons for rejection are a missing vehicle registration, vague timings, no reason given, a conflict with the digital tachograph and a late retrospective entry.
  • Record waiting time for the same period as the digital tachograph records it, and attach a time-stamped photo of the consignment note.
  • The same driver entry serves both as working time for payroll and as the basis for a surcharge on the freight invoice.

The driver records waiting time during a trailer swap as working time by noting the start and end time, the location of the terminal or port, the nature of the task (trailer swap, container swap or waiting for the load) and a reference such as the consignment note number. This guide shows step by step how to make the entry, what a sample entry that stands up to payroll and working time inspection looks like, and on what grounds a waiting time entry is rejected. Recording waiting time during trailer swaps is closely regulated, and done properly it protects both the driver's pay and the employer's invoicing.

Why is waiting time during a trailer swap working time?

Yes, it is. When a driver is swapping a trailer or container at a terminal or port and has to wait for loading, unloading or for the replacement unit to become available, this counts as working time, even though the vehicle is not moving and the driver is not doing physical work. In Finland, the rules on drivers' work are based on the requirements of the Working Hours Act 848/2019 and the Act on the working time of drivers: working time includes the time the driver is at the employer's disposal and cannot freely use their own time (Finnish Occupational Safety and Health Administration).

The practical significance of this rule is considerable. If the driver has left the terminal for an eight-hour regular daily rest but is woken to wait for the trailer to become available, that rest is no longer uninterrupted. The whole rest period is then broken and the driver is back on working time. This means that recording waiting time during trailer swaps is not a mere formality: it determines whether the rest is considered complete or not. Without an entry, the driver and the employer risk misreading the situation and breaching the working time rules.

When waiting time counts as working time and when it does not

Waiting counts as working time when the trailer swap is part of a task assigned by the employer and the driver has been instructed to be there. If, on the other hand, the driver waits at the terminal on their own initiative without an assignment, or is outside working hours, the time is not recorded. In borderline cases, what matters is whether the driver was at the employer's disposal. The entry can be made by hand or per vehicle in a system such as RAHTIS, where the stages of a job run from the driver all the way to invoicing.

In practice the difference is clear: if the transport planner has told the driver to go to the terminal and wait for a trailer swap, the waiting is working time from the outset. If, instead, the driver decides to stop at the terminal to wait for the next job without any specific instruction, the time cannot be recorded as working time. Likewise, if the driver has said they are reachable but is free to leave the vehicle and use their own time, this is a period of availability, which is subject to different rules.

What information must a waiting time entry include?

A rejected waiting time entry is almost always an incomplete one: it lacks the time, the place or the reason. The payroll administrator cannot accept a line saying "at terminal 2 h", because it does not show whether it was waiting for a trailer swap or some other delay.

To make the entry complete, the driver needs to know exactly which fields the payroll administrator and the inspector expect to see. The table below lists the required fields; if any is missing, the entry is rejected automatically. These fields must be filled in for every waiting time entry, whether a paper form, email or a transport management system is used.

Required fields

FieldExample
Start date and time14/3 at 09:15
End time14/3 at 11:40
LocationTerminal, street address or port berth
TaskTrailer swap: changing trailers
Order or job referenceReference to the consignment note or CMR note

Supporting details that speed up approval

A screenshot or time-stamped photo of the consignment note shortens the back-and-forth, as does the name of the consignee or the terminal supervisor. If the wait was caused by a queue, record the arrival time and the time shown on the display separately. When the driver records these straight away during the job, the transport planner does not have to fill in details afterwards, and the entry goes to payroll and invoicing as it stands. In RAHTIS the fields are completed using a template that also works on empty runs: see rahtis.eu/et.

Step by step: how the driver records waiting time during a trailer swap

Before arriving at the terminal

Record a time stamp as soon as you set off: take a photo or send a message on your phone showing your departure time and estimated arrival time at the terminal. Make sure the job instructions or consignment note include the customer's contact details so you can report a delay or an early arrival. If the load or trailer is not ready as agreed, report it before you arrive, so the reason for the wait can be verified from the start.

On arrival and when the wait begins

On arrival, record two things: the time and the place. In practice a time-stamped photo of the gate display, the gate screen or the yard, or a location-based entry in the app, is enough. Also record who is receiving you: the terminal name, gate number and any acknowledgement of your arrival. Tell reception you have arrived and ask them to confirm that the load or trailer is not ready, because it is exactly this confirmation that separates an accepted waiting time entry from a rejected one.

Directive 2002/15/EC distinguishes between periods of availability, when the driver must be present and reachable, and free time, when they may leave the vehicle; waiting during a trailer swap almost always falls into the first group and is therefore working time (European Commission summary of the working time directive). So record the start of the wait as soon as reception tells you the load is not there: do not wait to see whether it sorts itself out within the hour. Try recording waiting time in RAHTIS yourself: https://www.rahtis.eu/sv.

When the wait ends and recording what follows

Once the trailer has been swapped or the load secured, note the end time of the wait and continue the journey on the same entry. Finally, record the trailer or container number, the consignment note number and any acknowledgement from reception. The entry then forms a continuous chain: arrival, start of waiting, end of waiting and onward journey, all on the same job.

Sample entries: a trailer swap and waiting for a load

Example 1: trailer swap in the terminal yard

An accepted entry might look like this: "10/3, 09:15–10:40, trailer swap, terminal yard, Vantaa. Trailer change: empty trailer collected from the yard, loaded trailer dropped in its place, tractor unit and trailer recoupled. Witness: terminal shift supervisor." Record the time of arrival, not just the time the swap started.

Example 2: waiting at the gate before collecting a container

Another example: "10/3, 12:00 arrived at port gate, collection from the gate began at 13:30, container secured at 14:10. Reason for waiting: container had not yet been grounded." Here the waiting time spent at the gate is 1 h 30 min, and the entry shows the reason, so the person invoicing can claim compensation from the customer.

In both cases it is worth attaching a time-stamped photo of the gate display or the consignment note.
