When the same entry feeds directly into the job stages in RAHTIS, the driver does not copy information by hand, and the payroll administrator sees the waiting time in the same view as the rest of the job's records (https://www.rahtis.eu/lv).

The most common reasons for rejection in payroll

The most common reason for rejection is a missing vehicle or trailer registration: without a registration number, the payroll administrator cannot match the entry to the driving log record. The second is vague timing, such as just "all morning" with no start and end time. The third is a missing reason: an entry that only says "waiting terminal" does not show whether it was queuing because the load was being prepared or getting ready for the trailer swap.

The fourth reason is a conflict with the digital tachograph. If the tachograph shows rest for the same period for which the driver is claiming waiting time as working time, the payroll administrator will reject the entry unless it is a precisely defined exception. Traficom advises that discrepancies between working time records and the digital tachograph must be explainable at inspection, so it is worth adding an explanation when the entry is made (Traficom's working time guidance).

The fifth reason is a late retrospective entry made weeks afterwards. Avoid all five by recording the waiting time on the same day and adding the trailer swap details: terminal, container number and customer name. In RAHTIS the same entry is attached directly to the job, so invoicing and payroll see the same information without a separate email.

How does the entry stand up to a working time inspection?

The authorities compare waiting time entries with two sources: the driver's working time records and the vehicle's digital tachograph. Questions arise if the tachograph shows a stop during the trailer swap but nothing has been entered in the working time records, or the recorded time differs from the tachograph by hours.

Reconciling the digital tachograph and the manual entry

Record waiting time for the same period as the digital tachograph records. If the trailer swap started at 10:15 and ended at 12:45, the same times go into the working time records, not rounded hours. Explain in the entry why the vehicle was stationary: for example "queuing at terminal, container swap, collecting consignment note".

If the entry and the tachograph do not match, correct both on the same day and record the reason for the correction. Entries rejected in payroll are often ones where the driver's paper note and the system's time stamps differ with no explanation. When the entry, the tachograph and the payroll records tell the same story, the inspection goes through without questions.

The inspector may also ask for evidence that the wait was caused by the customer or the terminal and not by the driver's own delay. That is why photos of gate displays, emails from the sender or terminal receipts are worth their weight in gold. If the waiting time was interrupted by a break or rest, the inspector will want to see that the break was taken in accordance with the rules and that there are no gaps in the working time records. From the inspector's point of view, recording waiting time during trailer swaps is most reliable when every stop is explained and the driving schedule is consistent from departure to destination.

How does the transport planner handle waiting time entries in payroll?

In a small firm, the transport planner and the payroll administrator are often the same person, so it pays to process a waiting time entry as soon as the driver's record comes in. First check that the entry has a start and end time, the name of the terminal or port and the reason for waiting. If any of these is missing, ask for it to be completed the same day, not at the end of the payroll run.

Waiting time in customer invoicing and the freight rate

On the pay side, waiting time is recorded as working time according to the driver's employment contract or the sector's terms. On the invoicing side the basis is different: most haulage contracts and general conditions of carriage specify which waiting time is charged as a surcharge and on what basis, for example at an hourly rate after a period of free waiting time. The guidance of SKAL (the Finnish Transport and Logistics association) on invoicing waiting time and freight surcharges explains at what point the right to a surcharge arises and how it is documented (SKAL).

In practice, then, the same entry is used twice: as working time for payroll and as a surcharge on the freight invoice. When both are based on the same driver entry, the figures also match at inspection.

How does RAHTIS support recording and invoicing waiting time?

RAHTIS is built so that the driver records waiting time directly on the job: the start and end time, the type of swap (trailer or container), the location and a free-text description of what happened are saved in the same workflow that the shipper follows step by step. The entry does not stay on paper or in a separate app; the transport planner sees it immediately and it travels on with the job. When the job is completed, the waiting time details are part of the same package as the consignment note and the POD, so invoicing is based on saved records rather than memory. This removes the typical problem of waiting time only coming to light when someone asks about it after the invoice has gone out.

Where RAHTIS does not help (yet)

RAHTIS does not calculate the price of waiting time compensation for you, nor does it know the contract terms of each customer: you set the price and terms yourself, as you do now. Nor does the system replace the driver's own working time records on the tachograph or payroll side; it produces entries that you transfer to your own payroll.

FAQ

Does the customer pay for waiting time if the trailer swap is delayed for reasons on the terminal's side?

Often, yes, but the basis lies in the contract, not in the driver's entry. General conditions of carriage and haulage contracts specify a period of free waiting time, after which the right to a surcharge arises. Record the reason for the delay, the start and end time and the order reference, so that invoicing can base the surcharge on saved data rather than memory.

Is the digital tachograph enough as evidence of waiting time, or is a separate entry needed?

A separate entry is needed. The digital tachograph shows that the vehicle was stationary, but not the reason or the task. The inspector will have questions if the stop on the tachograph and the working time records do not match. Record the same times, the location, the type of swap and a reference to the consignment note, so that any discrepancy can be explained afterwards.

What do I do if the terminal will not give arrival or release times in writing?

Record the times yourself on the same day and add your own evidence: a time-stamped photo of the consignment note, the name of the consignee or terminal supervisor and the container number. If the wait was caused by a queue, note the arrival time and the time shown on the display separately. These supporting details speed up approval even when the terminal confirms nothing in writing.

Is waiting time during a trailer swap recorded as working time for the driver of the vehicle or for the driver doing the swap?

The entry goes into the working time records of the driver who was at the employer's disposal during the wait. If the driver of the replacement vehicle waits on site as instructed, the time is their working time. What decides it is not the vehicle's registration number but who was instructed to be there and whose free time the wait restricted.

How much waiting time is paid to the driver in full, and when is it treated as a break?

No general limit for full payment can be given without an employment contract or the sector's terms: on the pay side, your own contract terms decide. On the tachograph side, a long stationary period can easily turn into rest, so that the working time claim and the tachograph conflict. Record the start and end of the wait accurately and explain in the entry in advance how breaks fit in.

pienen-kuljetusfirman-ajopaivakirja-sahk.title: An electronic driving log for a small haulage firm's drivers
pienen-kuljetusfirman-ajopaivakirja-sahk.description: An electronic driving log for a small haulage firm's drivers: up and running in six weeks, with data going straight to invoicing and no IT budget.
pienen-kuljetusfirman-ajopaivakirja-sahk.html:
Key takeaways

  • The law does not require paper: an electronic driving log is acceptable as long as the data is complete, reliable and can be checked afterwards.
  • A realistic budget for a firm with 1–10 vehicles is from tens to hundreds of euros a month, and per-vehicle pricing is usually the fairest model.
  • The logging app must work offline, open with a single tap and take less than a minute, or paper will be back in the cab.
  • Six weeks is enough to move from paper to electronic: selection and pilot, two weeks of running both in parallel, then retiring paper.
  • The same electronic entry serves the driving log, the consignment note, invoicing and payroll without copying.

A small haulage firm introduces an electronic driving log by choosing a phone-based logging app, making sure the data meets the statutory requirements, training drivers to log their own journeys and linking the data directly to invoicing and payroll. This guide shows step by step how a firm with 1–12 lorries makes the switch without an IT budget and without finally ditching paper until the electronic version has been proven to work.

Why should a small haulage firm digitise its driving log?

When you are the firm's transport planner, bookkeeper and safety manager all at once, every paper driving log is work you will have to sort out yourself later. An electronic driving log moves the recording to the driver at the moment the journey happens, and the data is ready at the same time for invoicing, payroll and working time monitoring.

Where the paper log breaks down in practice

On paper the handwriting is illegible, hours are missing or the sheet stays in the cab for a week. The requirements for drivers' logs and working time records are laid down in law, and the Finnish Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment's guidance on working hours requires that the data can be verified afterwards. When the paper is poor, you end up correcting it in the evenings.

Time saved by linking dispatch and invoicing

When journeys, consignment note data and paid hours live in the same system, you do not copy anything twice. RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/fi) combines job tracking and invoicing in one place, so instead of a paper log the invoice goes out straight from the recorded journeys. The same data also serves payroll without a separate home-made Excel set-up.

What does the law require of a driving log, and is an electronic version accepted?

Working time legislation and the driver's log

In Finland, records of drivers' working time are based on data from the vehicle's tachograph or the digital driver card, but the employer must also keep working time records covering, among other things, other work, unpaid time and daily rest. The driving log supplements this: it documents the route, load and mode of transport of each individual job. The law does not specify whether records are kept on paper or electronically, as long as the data is complete, reliable and can be checked afterwards. An electronic driving log is therefore acceptable if it produces the same information as the paper version.

Evidential value and archiving of electronic data

Evidential value is decisive in disputes: a customer questions the delivery time or a shipper questions the content of the consignment note. An electronic log contains a time stamp, the driver's identifier and an unalterable history, which is clearer evidence than paper. Retention obligations are worth checking with your own accountant, but in practice the data has to be kept in the business for several years. In RAHTIS the driving log, consignment note and POD are linked to the same job, so the evidence is in one place rather than in separate folders (https://www.rahtis.eu/et). Remember that it must also be possible to show the driver's signature and the vehicle identifier afterwards.

What does an electronic driving log cost a small firm?

A realistic budget for a firm with 1–10 vehicles is from tens to hundreds of euros a month. The cost is made up of the software licence, the drivers' phones and your own time: installation, training and changing habits often cost more than the licences.

Pricing models: per vehicle, per user, fixed

ModelYou payBest suited toRisk
Per vehicleFixed sum / lorry / monthPredictable cost when drivers changeIdle months still cost money if the fleet shrinks
Per userSum / user / monthSmall fleet, many people loggingCost rises as you take on more staff
Fixed packageContract price / monthEstablished fleet and staffOversized if the firm shrinks

In a small firm, per vehicle is usually the fairest: the fleet is what earns the money. RAHTIS pricing follows this principle and suits firms from a single lorry upwards (https://www.rahtis.eu/lv).

Hidden costs: training, devices, integrations

Three items are often left out of the budget. Training drivers takes working days, and every new person logging needs to be inducted again. Devices: if logging is done on the driver's own phone, the cost is zero; company tablets cost €200–400 each. Integrations with invoicing and payroll are free when built in, but expensive when custom-made.

Remember the archiving obligation too: the regulation on drivers' working time (EC 561/2006) requires data to be kept, so choose a service you can also get your data out of after the contract ends (EU Regulation 561/2006, EUR-Lex).

How do you choose an electronic driving log without an IT department?

Selection criteria for a small firm

When you are the transport planner, invoicing clerk and safety manager yourself, choose a solution against five criteria: can you use it on a phone without training, do you see entries in real time, does the data go straight to invoicing, does it work without a separate server, and is the pricing per vehicle rather than per user? Test each candidate on one real job, not a demo: log one loose trailer move, one consignment note and one empty run from start to finish. If installation needs a consultant or hours of learning, give it a miss.

Where RAHTIS meets these criteria and where it does not

RAHTIS is designed for firms from a single lorry upwards: the driver logs the journey on a phone, and the same data is visible to you and goes to invoicing without copying from paper. Combining a freight exchange with transport management removes separate logins and paper notes about who owes what. You can apply at https://www.rahtis.eu/sv/apply.

To be honest: RAHTIS does not replace the statutory data from the tachograph, and it is not a fuel or maintenance system for heavy vehicles. If all you need is tachograph download software, other tools will do.

How do you get drivers on board with the new way of logging journeys?

Mobile logging that copes with terminal routines

Logging is done on a phone, with gloves on, dirty screens and a poor signal. The solution must work offline, open with a single tap and ask only for the essential fields: origin, destination, load and job status. If logging takes more than a minute, it will not get done and paper will go back in the pocket.

Allow drivers their own way of working too: one logs at every stop, another at the end of the day. What matters most is that the data is created out on the road, not afterwards in the office from memory.

Ground rules for the transition period

Run both in parallel for two weeks: paper and electronic logging at the same time. This gives you comparison data and drivers learn without pressure. Agree on one rule: notes may be written on paper, but the official record is electronic, and missing entries are sorted out the same day, not a week later.

Remember the archiving obligation: in Finland electronic documents must be kept for the period laid down in the Accounting Act, and their evidential value requires the data to be unalterable and traceable (Vero.fi, the Finnish Tax Administration, on keeping electronic records). Once logging is in order, the data flows on to RAHTIS for invoicing, and free vehicles are matched directly to freight exchange jobs on the application page.

How does driving log data get to invoicing and payroll?

Journey data to the consignment note and the invoice

When journey logging is electronic, the same entry can work in three places: as the driver's log, as an attachment to the consignment note and as the basis for invoicing. In practice the driver logs the job, the kilometres and waiting times, and the system links them to the order. In RAHTIS the consignment note and journey data are in the same workflow, so the invoice can be raised directly from the logged journey without copying from paper into Excel.

An honest limitation: RAHTIS does not send invoices directly to an e-invoicing operator, so invoices are exported to your accounting software as a file. That is still quicker than typing them up from paper notes.

Working time and payroll

The same entry also works as a working time report. The driver's journeys, breaks and other work are saved with time stamps, and at the end of the month you send a ready-made report to payroll instead of a wallet full of paper slips. Digital logging is also more accurate: checks based on the vehicle's speed data reveal missing entries that on paper only come to light at inspection.

If you use separate payroll software, check before choosing which file format you can use to transfer working time data into it.

How do you move from paper to electronic step by step?

Six weeks is enough if the job is split into three two-week blocks: selection and pilot, parallel running and finally retiring paper. The aim is that no job goes unlogged by falling into a gap between the two systems during the transition.

Weeks 1–2: selection and pilot

Choose a solution using the selection criteria (previous section) in week 1 and put one driver on trial. Only one lorry's journeys are logged electronically; paper is not removed yet. At the same time, check the driving log guidance from SKAL and the Finnish Transport Employers' Association so the data you record is correct from the start: keeping a driving log. In week 2, go over with the pilot driver what worked and what felt like pointless tapping.

Weeks 3–4: parallel running

All vehicles now log both on paper and electronically. This is the most time-consuming phase, but it exposes the situations where the app does not fit the real work: waiting for loading, no signal in the yard, the change of day falling in the middle of a job. Compare the paper and electronic versions daily and fix logging habits immediately rather than collecting corrections on a list.

Weeks 5–6: retiring paper for good

The paper version stays in the vehicle as a backup, but it is no longer filled in. Drivers log only electronically, and you check the entries at the end of the day before invoicing. Once two full weeks have gone by with no missing entries and invoices have been produced from the driving log data without any separate reconciling, paper can be dropped completely. Keep one completed paper form as a reference point in case the tax authority or an inspector asks questions later.

Summary: where to start today?

Pick one vehicle and one driver, and log next week electronically alongside paper. Check that the data flows straight from the consignment note to invoicing without retyping. If everything goes through, extend it to a second vehicle and drop paper altogether within a month.

RAHTIS is designed for exactly this: from a single lorry upwards, with dispatch, driving log and invoicing in one place and no separate IT budget. Try it in practice and see whether it fits the way you run your jobs.

FAQ

Can the driving log still be kept on paper if drivers refuse to use a mobile app?

Yes, because the law does not prescribe the form of the records, as long as the data is complete and can be checked afterwards. Paper, however, requires constant correcting and chasing: illegible handwriting, missing hours and late forms end up being fixed by you. Two weeks of parallel running lowers the threshold, and most drivers get used to logging on a phone when it takes less than a minute and works offline.

Does an electronic driving log work without a signal at a terminal or abroad?

Yes, if you choose an app that logs offline and uploads the data later. The signal at terminals is often weak, so the log must open with a single tap and save locally on the phone. Test this during the pilot on one real job, not a demo: log one loose trailer move and one empty run from start to finish. If logging gets stuck waiting for a connection, paper will soon be back in the cab.

Does a small firm need separate driving log software, or is a TMS with logging built in enough?

A dedicated, separate program rarely makes sense for a firm with 1–12 lorries. It is enough for logging to be part of the same workflow as the consignment note and invoicing, so the same entry serves the driving log, the invoice and payroll without copying. Choose a solution against five criteria: phone use without training, real-time visibility, direct transfer to invoicing, no server, and per-vehicle pricing.

How long does the law require driving log data to be archived?

In practice the data must be kept in the business for several years, and the exact retention period is best confirmed with your own accountant. The EU regulation on drivers' working time, 561/2006, also requires data to be kept, and in Finland the Accounting Act lays down retention periods for electronic documents. Before choosing, make sure you can get all your data out of the service even after the contract ends, so that the archiving obligation does not depend on the app.

How are incorrect entries made by drivers corrected afterwards?

Agree a rule that missing or wrongly logged journeys are sorted out the same day, not a week later. In a good system a correction leaves a time-stamped trace in the unalterable history, which preserves the evidential value of the records in a dispute. Check the entries yourself at the end of the day before invoicing, so errors do not make it onto the invoice and the driver gets feedback straight away.

rahtilaskujen-hoito-ilman-jalkikaiteista.title: Freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact
rahtilaskujen-hoito-ilman-jalkikaiteista.description: Freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact: the order, sign-off and POD go straight into the invoice, so it can go out as soon as goods are delivered.
rahtilaskujen-hoito-ilman-jalkikaiteista.html:
Key takeaways

  • A paperless freight invoicing process relies on recording the job details once, with the same record flowing from the order to the consignment note, the driver's sign-off and the finished invoice.
  • An electronic freight invoice must contain the same mandatory details as a paper invoice, and in Finland invoices must be kept for at least six years from the end of the financial year.
  • The driver's mobile sign-off and the POD attachment are linked to the invoice automatically, which does away with envelopes of receipts scanned after the fact and speeds up payment.
  • Freight exchange and loose trailer jobs fit into the same invoicing process when each customer receives its own invoice with its own terms and references.
  • RAHTIS does not replace accounting software: the balance sheet and annual accounts are still handled by your accountant, who gets the data directly from the system.

You can handle freight invoices without paperwork after the fact when the consignment note details, the driver's sign-off and the POD attachment go straight from the system into the invoice: the order is created once, the driver signs off the job on a mobile and the invoice is produced complete with attachments. This guide goes through the whole life cycle from order to archiving, including loose trailer and freight exchange jobs.

What does freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact mean?

A paperless freight invoicing process means that the job details are created once in the system and go straight from there into the invoice: the order, route, driver's sign-off, POD attachment and consignment note details in a single chain. The invoice is produced ready for the archive, and you do not have to spend an evening going through envelopes of receipts and notes.

For a small business the benefit is tangible: when dispatching, invoicing and bookkeeping are all handled by the same person, every line typed by hand takes time that is lost elsewhere. According to the Finnish Tax Administration, an electronic invoice must contain the same mandatory details as a paper invoice, so the law does not force you to use paper (Finnish Tax Administration). In RAHTIS the shipper publishes the job once and the driver signs off each stage directly, so the invoice material is ready before the lorry is back at base. In practice the process starts with the customer's job or the freight exchange job being entered once, not in three places.

The essence of going paperless is not the technology itself but joining the information flows into a single chain in which the same data is never entered twice. When the driver signs off the delivery in the mobile app, the sign-off does not disappear into an inbox waiting for a separate invoicing round; it triggers the invoice automatically. This means the invoice can be in the customer's inbox or online bank before the driver has even made it back home. With the traditional model this would be impossible, because invoicing always depends on the paper consignment note coming back and the data being entered into the system by hand. In a paperless process that delay disappears and the invoicing lead time shrinks from days to hours, which significantly improves the company's cash flow.

What requirements apply to an electronic freight invoice in Finland?

Mandatory invoice details

The Finnish VAT Act sets out what every freight invoice must contain: the names and details of the seller and the buyer, the Business ID or other identifier, the invoice number, the date, the date or period of supply, the quantity and nature of the goods or services, the VAT rate, the amount payable and the payment terms. Whether the job comes via a freight exchange or from your own customer, the same fields are filled in every time. In RAHTIS the order and consignment note details serve as the source data, so the mandatory fields fill themselves in without a separate paper form. If you invoice abroad, for example a Swedish or German customer, the details are the same, but the language and references are worth checking at the order stage. You can try it out in practice at Pieteikums · RAHTIS.

In addition to the mandatory invoice details, the haulage sector has its own specific requirements that general invoicing software does not always cover. A freight invoice often includes a reference number linking it to a particular job or transport contract, plus a breakdown of surcharges such as waiting time, unloading delays or ADR surcharges. Itemising these by hand on a paper invoice or in general invoicing software is laborious and error-prone. When the source data comes straight from the transport management system, the breakdown is generated automatically from the prices agreed with the order and the extra events recorded during the transport. This reduces customers' questions about the content of the invoice and speeds up payment.

Archiving and retention period

Under the Finnish Accounting Act, invoices and accounting material must be kept for at least six years from the end of the financial year, and the financial statements material for seven years. Electronic archiving is permitted as long as the data remains unaltered and accessible throughout the retention period. In practice this means POD attachments, consignment note details and invoices can live in the same system without cardboard files. When the driver's sign-off and attachment have been linked to the job during the transport, archiving happens at the same time, and no one is left with paperwork after the fact.

For retention requirements, what matters is that the electronic archive is protected against changes and its data is traceable. The system must be able to show when the invoice was created, when the attachments were added and who signed them off. RAHTIS stores the time stamp and user for every event, so the audit trail is in order without a separate log book. If the tax authority asks for evidence of a particular job from three years ago, the whole set is in one place: the invoice, consignment note, POD attachment and the driver's sign-off with time stamps. In the paper world the same job might be scattered across three or four files in different offices, and some of the information could be missing or hard to read.

How do you get freight invoice data straight from the transport management system into the invoice?

Order stage: getting the job details right once

The chain starts with the order: the customer's email or a freight exchange job is turned into a transport task in the system, with the collection and delivery addresses, load description, freight rate, surcharges (such as waiting time or ADR) and payment terms. This data is saved once and reused at every stage: for the consignment note, the driver's task list and finally the invoice. Eliminating retyping is the core of the whole chain, because every line copied by hand is one more possible error on the invoice and one more reason for the customer to pay late.

In practice this means that when you enter a job in RAHTIS, the same record goes with it all the way: from the order to the consignment note details, the driver's sign-offs and the finished invoice line. You do not have to dig the agreed price out of a notebook later or check scraps of paper, because everything is already in the same record. The system does not replace dispatching decisions; it simply makes sure that data entered once is not lost on its way to the invoice.

The quality of the data created at the order stage determines whether the whole chain works. If an address is incomplete or the freight rate is missing, these gaps carry through to the consignment note and the invoice, so the first entry has to be made carefully. In practice it pays to create order templates for different types of customer: a regular customer with fixed routes and prices, a freight exchange job where prices vary, and a one-off job where everything is entered by hand. Once the template is ready, the mandatory fields are filled in by default and only exceptions need manual input. This halves the time spent on orders and reduces the risk of entry errors, because the system will not let a job go forward without the mandatory details.

Consignment note details as the basis for the invoice

The consignment note (CMR) is filled in from the same record, and once the driver signs off the delivery and the POD attachment has been saved, the invoice is produced without a separate step. The invoice shows the customer details, freight rate, surcharges and attachments, all derived from the original order and the events of the transport. Retention obligations are best checked directly in official guidance, such as on the Finnish Tax Administration's website, so that archiving is done correctly from the start.

The consignment note details form the basis of the invoice because they contain what actually happened during the transport: loading and unloading times, any damage or discrepancies, and the consignee's acknowledgement. When this data comes straight from the system, the invoice is based not just on the order but on verifiable events. If the customer claims the delivery was late, the time stamp of unloading attached to the invoice shows when it actually happened. If the freight rate includes waiting time, the driver's sign-off verifies how long the wait lasted. This chain from order to consignment note to invoice is what makes freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact possible: every invoice line can be traced to a concrete event, not to a note or a receipt.

How are the driver's sign-offs and attachments added to a digital freight invoice?

POD and CMR sign-off on mobile

Straight after unloading, the driver photographs the signed CMR or consignment note on their phone and marks the load as delivered in the app. The photo, time stamp and location are saved directly to that job, so paper copies do not have to be posted back or scanned at the office in the evening. If the consignee insists on a paper acknowledgement, a photographed document is enough as an invoice attachment for most customers.

How easy the driver's mobile app is to use determines how likely the sign-off is to be done correctly and on time. If the app is slow or needs lots of fields filled in, the driver puts the sign-off off until the evening or forgets it altogether, and invoicing is delayed. The RAHTIS mobile sign-off is designed around the bare minimum: the job opens, the driver takes a photo, the consignee signs on the screen and the job is marked as complete. The location and time stamp are saved in the background with no extra step. This means the sign-off is done before the driver starts the engine at the delivery point, and the invoice material is ready straight away.

Automatically linking attachments to the invoice

When the job is marked as complete, the system gathers the POD photo, the CMR sign-off and any other attachments into the same record from which the invoice is produced. The invoicing software does not have to ask for attachments separately afterwards, and they do not need to be attached by hand via email. In RAHTIS the driver's sign-off is visible to the customer step by step, and the completed POD is attached to the invoice automatically (https://www.rahtis.eu/lt). This removes the most common reason for payment disputes: the customer cannot claim that the delivery document is missing.

An honest limitation: if the customer requires the original paper CMR to be posted, a digital image only partly replaces it, and the original must still be kept.

Automatically linking attachments means in practice that the invoice is not a separate document but part of the job record. When the invoice goes to the customer, the POD attachment, the CMR photo and any additional explanations go with it, without anyone having to put them together separately. This is a significant difference from the traditional model, where invoicing is a separate step that needs its own attachments, its own email and its own archiving. In RAHTIS these are parts of the same record, and sending the invoice takes one click because all the supporting material is already in place.

How do loose trailer and freight exchange jobs fit into the same invoicing process?

Loose trailer work should not be a separate invoicing channel. When freight exchange jobs and your own customers go through the same system, filling empty legs and invoicing are handled without a notebook or a paper CMR.

Freight exchange job details straight into the system

When you take a job from a freight exchange, the customer details, route and freight are entered once, not afterwards from a receipt. In RAHTIS the driver signs off collection and delivery, the POD attachment is saved with the job and the consignment note details complete the invoice template. Electronic consignment notes are permitted in the EU under the Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention (UNECE e-CMR page), so there is no need to carry paper.

The catch with loose trailer jobs is that customers change and invoice terms vary: one pays at 14 days, another at 30 days, a third requires its own reference number system. When this information is recorded with the job, the invoice adapts automatically to each customer's requirements without you having to remember who pays on which terms. This is particularly important when you run a mix of jobs: your own customers, jobs from Trans.eu and jobs agreed directly by phone, all in the same week. If invoicing is a separate process, you have to check each job's terms individually, which takes longer than the driving itself.

Invoicing several customers

Each customer receives its own invoice with its own terms and references, even if the jobs are in the same calendar. When the POD and consignment note are already attached, the invoice can be sent as soon as the goods are delivered, and a later empty leg that gets filled is handled in the same way. RAHTIS handles both the same way; more information and application: Заявка · RAHTIS.

Managing several customers requires the system to keep jobs clearly apart: who ordered it, what the route is, what the price is and when the invoice falls due. When this information is in the same calendar, you can see at a glance which invoices have been sent and which are waiting. This prevents double invoicing and forgotten jobs, which are the most common mistakes in a paper-based process. And when filling empty legs is part of the same system, invoicing those legs follows the same logic: the driver signs off the collection, the invoice is produced and the POD is attached automatically.

How are archiving and inspections handled without a paper archive?

When freight invoice data, the driver's sign-offs and POD attachments build up in the same system, the archive creates itself as you work. Every job remains searchable: the consignment note details, attachments and invoice can be found by customer or registration number in seconds, with no safe or old files.

Payment tracking without a notebook

You can see the status of each invoice directly in the system: sent, paid, overdue. Instead of recording "who owes what" in a paper notebook, RAHTIS tracks payment dates job by job and flags the overdue ones. You can send payment reminders without a separate Excel file, and your accountant gets the data straight from the system instead of scraps of paper.

Effective payment tracking depends on the system knowing the status of every invoice in real time. When the invoice goes out, the status is "sent". When payment arrives, it changes to "paid". If the due date passes, the status changes to "overdue" and the system flags it without you having to go through a list by hand. This is a significant advantage over Excel-based tracking, where the status has to be updated by hand and overdue invoices can go unnoticed for weeks. In RAHTIS overdue invoices appear in a separate view from which you can send a payment reminder with one click, without having to look up the original invoice or the customer's contact details separately.

Responding to inspections from a digital archive

When the tax authority or customs asks for documents, digging through years-old piles of paper becomes a search. You select the period and the customer, and the system lists the consignment notes, POD attachments and invoices. The same applies to disputes with customers: if the other party claims a delivery is missing, the sign-off time stamp and the POD attachment can be shown in moments. RAHTIS keeps the archive in order automatically, but final responsibility for retention obligations and tax treatment lies with you and your accountant, as with any system.

In an inspection, speed and completeness are what count. If the tax authority gives you a week to supply invoices and related documents for a three-month period, putting them together from a paper archive can take a whole day. From a digital archive the same material is put together in minutes: you select the period, filter by customer and the system lists everything, including attachments. This not only saves time but also reduces the risk of errors, because documents can get lost or mixed up when gathered by hand. What is more, the digital archive is always in the same format and in the same place, so responding to different inspectors' requests is consistent and quick.

What should you bear in mind when moving from paper to electronic freight invoices?

Making the switch in 30 days

Week 1: choose one customer and one type of job for a pilot. Week 2: enter open jobs into the system and link the consignment note details directly to the invoice. Week 3: introduce driver sign-offs and POD attachments so the attachments follow the invoice automatically. Week 4: invoice the pilot customer electronically and check what is missing before moving everything else across.

Keep a paper CMR in the vehicle as a backup for the first month. Finnish Customs and the Finnish Tax Administration may require transport documents during inspections, so check the retention periods directly on the Finnish Tax Administration's website.

A successful switch depends on the driver learning the new way quickly and the customer accepting a digital invoice without resistance. For the driver, go through the mobile sign-off steps before the first job: open the app, select the job, take a photo, ask for a signature, mark as complete. Once learnt, the whole thing takes 30 seconds. For the customer, agree in advance that the invoice will come electronically with a photographed CMR attached rather than a paper one. Most customers accept this because it speeds up their own invoice processing. If a customer insists on a paper invoice, it is worth checking whether this is a real requirement or just habit, since in most cases it is habit rather than a legal requirement.

Where RAHTIS is not (yet) a fit

RAHTIS handles a job from order to archiving in one place, and it is designed to work right down to the owner-driver with a single lorry. But to be honest: RAHTIS is not a full accounting system, so the balance sheet and annual accounts are still handled by your accountant or in accounting software. If you run international loose trailer work through several freight exchanges, ask us directly about integrations with the different platforms before committing.

How do different tools compare for paperless freight invoicing?

The choice depends on whether you need a freight exchange, a transport management system or both in one place. A table from the small haulier's point of view:

An honest weakness: RAHTIS does not replace accounting software and may not cover every exchange job if your customers require a particular system. For hauliers who rely mainly on exchanges, Teleroute or Trans.eu may be the primary place to find work, with invoicing handled on the TMS side.

Your choice of tools also depends on how many different systems you are prepared to use every day. If you find jobs on Trans.eu, run them in Transportial and invoice in Excel, you have three different systems that do not talk to each other. That means every piece of data is moved by hand at least twice, which is exactly the paperwork marathon that going paperless is meant to eliminate. The strength of RAHTIS is that it combines the freight exchange and the TMS in one place, so finding, running and invoicing a job happen in a single chain. This does not mean RAHTIS replaces jobs from all the other exchanges, but it does mean that jobs coming through RAHTIS need no separate invoicing work. More information and the application form are at Ansökan · RAHTIS.

FAQ

How much time should paperless invoicing save a small firm?

This guide does not give an exact number of minutes, but the saving comes from data entered once not being copied again from the order to the consignment note and the invoice. When dispatching, invoicing and collecting POD attachments are handled in the same chain, going through and scanning envelopes of receipts in the afternoons disappears altogether, and the invoice can be sent as soon as the goods are delivered.

Is a photographed CMR enough as an invoice attachment?

For most customers it is, but not for all. If the consignee or customer requires the original paper CMR, a digital image only partly replaces it, and the original document must still be kept. That is why it is worth keeping a paper CMR in the vehicle as a backup, especially during the first month of the switch, and agreeing the method of sign-off with the customer in advance.

How long must invoices and attachments be kept?

Under the Finnish Accounting Act, invoices and accounting material are kept for at least six years from the end of the financial year, and financial statements material for seven years. An electronic archive is acceptable as long as the data remains unaltered and accessible throughout. Final responsibility for retention obligations lies with you and your accountant, even if the system handles archiving automatically.

Does RAHTIS replace accounting software?

No. RAHTIS handles a job from order to archiving: the order, consignment note details, driver sign-offs, POD attachments, the invoice and payment tracking. The balance sheet and annual accounts are still handled by your accountant or in accounting software, which gets the data directly from the system. So your accountant still needs their own tools, but no longer scraps of paper about jobs.

Do freight exchange jobs fit into the same invoicing process?

Yes. A job taken from an exchange is entered into the system once, with the customer, route and freight rate, and the driver signs off collection and delivery just as for your own customers. Each customer receives its own invoice with its own terms and references, even if the jobs are in the same calendar, and the POD attachment is linked to the invoice automatically.

rr-seuranta-noudosta-toimitukseen.title: RR tracking: following an order from collection to delivery
rr-seuranta-noudosta-toimitukseen.description: RR tracking shows an order's progress from collection to delivery without GPS units: customers check the status themselves, so fewer calls and notes.
rr-seuranta-noudosta-toimitukseen.html:
Key takeaways

  • RR tracking means following each order stage by stage from collection to delivery, not real-time vehicle location data.
  • Order tracking does not need GPS units, so for a small fleet it is a cheaper and lighter option.
  • Five pieces of information are enough for the customer: status, schedule, exceptions, consignment note number and POD.
  • In loose trailer and container work, the swap is recorded as a separate event so tracking does not break off mid-journey.
  • The biggest problem when introducing it is a status that is not updated, which is solved by making an update a single tap.

RR tracking means order-by-order tracking in which the transport moves through clear statuses: collection, load, swap, delivery and confirmation of the consignment note (POD). This guide shows how to set up the workflow so the customer can see the situation themselves and you save on phone calls, notes and spreadsheets, even if you run loose trailers or swap containers.

What does RR tracking mean in practice?

RR tracking means order-based tracking: a single consignment is followed step by step from collection to delivery, rather than the lorry's position on a map. In other words, it is about transport events, such as loading, unloading and the consignment note coming back, not vehicle location data.

The distinction matters because many small hauliers currently track only their own lorry or phone the customer to ask about the load. With order tracking, the customer can see what stage their particular job has reached, and the driver marks the stages along the way. The consignment note, or CMR, underpins the process: it is the contract that sets out the collection and delivery stages and the liability under the CMR Convention.

In practice RR tracking can work without a separate GPS system: the driver updates the status, and a system such as RAHTIS (https://www.rahtis.eu/) shows the order's progress all the way to the customer.

How does RR tracking differ from real-time vehicle tracking?

RR tracking means status-based tracking: the transport progresses stage by stage from collection to delivery, and the customer can see where their own consignment is. GPS-based vehicle tracking, on the other hand, follows the lorry, not the load. The same lorry may carry three different orders in a day, in which case vehicle tracking tells you where the lorry is, but not whose consignment is on board.

For a small firm, status tracking is often enough, because it tells the customer exactly what they ask on the phone: has the load been collected, is it on its way and has it been delivered. A GPS system adds devices, monthly fees and maintenance, the benefit of which is small for a small fleet.

RR tracking (per order)GPS tracking (per vehicle)
What is trackedAn individual consignmentThe vehicle
Customer visibilityTheir own order, stage by stagePosition of the whole lorry
Needs a deviceNoYes
Best suited toFirms with 1–12 vehiclesLarge fleets

In RAHTIS, RR tracking is built straight into the order: you record the stages yourself or the driver marks them, with no separate GPS system. Under the terms of use, responsibility for reporting the status always lies with the haulier, so accurate stage recording also protects you in disputes (https://www.rahtis.eu/en/terms).

When GPS tracking is still needed

GPS tracking is worthwhile if your customer requires real-time lorry location written into the contract, if you run vehicle operating hours or service intervals from the system, or if your fleet is spread across several drivers and you want a fleet manager's view. Theft risk and mandatory monitoring of drivers' working time can also justify a device. In other cases, status tracking meets the customer's needs more cheaply and with less hassle.

What information should you show the customer in order tracking?

The customer needs five things: the current status (collected, in transit, delivered), the estimated schedule, exceptions such as a delay or rerouting, the consignment note number and the POD once the signed delivery note has reached the system. This is enough to eliminate almost every customer service call: when the customer can see the status themselves, they do not ring to ask "where's the lorry?".

Avoid showing the driver's personal details, precise real-time coordinates, freight rates or other customers on the same route. EU rules also limit what vehicle location data may be passed on; the Commission's rules on tachographs set out what location data may be used for (EUR-Lex, rules on vehicle positioning devices).

In practice you share a link with the customer that shows only that order's details. In RAHTIS this works by the order progressing from collection to delivery while the customer sees the same status as you do in the dispatch view; the API documentation describes how status data can be shared with the customer's own systems (https://www.rahtis.eu/en/api-docs). An honest limitation: RAHTIS does not show a map accurate to the minute – tracking is based on status updates, which is enough for most loose trailer and job-by-job transport.

How are one-off jobs, such as loose trailer and container transport, tracked stage by stage?

RR tracking for loose trailer and container transport is built on four stages: publication, collection, swap and delivery. Each stage is updated as soon as the driver or the transport planner records the event, so the customer can see the situation without phone calls.

Stage 1: publishing and accepting the task

The job is published once, either on the freight exchange or directly to the customer: collection point, destination, vehicle requirement and schedule. Once accepted, the task gets its own reference, around which all later information builds up. A task published in RAHTIS goes straight into your own workflow, so there is no need for separate exchange records or copying into a spreadsheet.

Stage 2: collection and load confirmation

The driver records arrival at the collection point, and loading is confirmed either in the app or with the consignment note details. At this stage it is worth recording the container or trailer number, because it is the only sure way to identify the right unit when the same equipment is used on several jobs. An incorrect container number is the most common reason RR tracking shows the wrong route.

Stage 3: swaps and intermediate statuses

In container and loose trailer traffic the load often changes vehicle mid-journey: at a port, a terminal or a partner's yard. The swap is recorded as a separate event, so the time stamps are kept and the customer can see what stage the load is at even when the vehicle changes. Without recording these intermediate stages, tracking breaks off at exactly the points where customers ask most often.

Stage 4: delivery and POD

Delivery is confirmed with a POD: a receipt, signature or photo is attached directly to the task. RAHTIS combines the consignment note, POD and invoicing in the same record, so invoicing follows delivery automatically. Through the API (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/api-docs) the status can also be passed on to the customer's own system.

How is tracking information shared with the customer automatically?

There are three practical ways: a shared tracking link, email notifications when the status changes and API integration. For most firms with 1–12 vehicles, the first two are enough.

Shared link vs. email notifications

A shared link is the simplest way: once the order is in RAHTIS, you send the customer a link through which they can see the status from collection to delivery. You do not call, the customer does not call you, and you can send the link once and forget about it. Email notifications work when the customer cannot be bothered to click anything: the system sends a message automatically when the status changes, for example "collected" or "delivered".

A shared link has one honest limitation: the customer sees the status only when you update it. If you forget to mark the collection as done, the customer sees out-of-date information. That is why the status is best updated on the phone while on the road, not in a notebook at home in the evening.

API integration

API integration means tracking data goes straight into the customer's own system without emails or links. It is mainly relevant when your customer is large and needs the data in its own system. For a small haulier this is rarely the first step, and RAHTIS does not yet offer an open API for customer integrations, so it is worth coming back to this only when a larger customer account requires it.

Freight exchanges such as Teleroute and Trans.eu handle offers and address details for one-off jobs, but they do not track a job from collection to delivery in a way the customer can see. That is why final order tracking and customer communication are best kept in your own systems, not behind an exchange login.

What are the most common tracking problems and how are they solved?

The biggest problem is the driver not updating the status. The solution is to make updating so easy that it needs no call to the transport planner: a single tap on the mobile says that the lorry is at the collection point, loaded or unloaded. When the status is updated from the road, dispatch can see the situation without notes.

The second problem is an exception that goes unreported: a delay, damage or a wrong address. When the order is tracked stage by stage from collection to delivery, the exception is recorded on the same order with a time stamp, so you can tell the customer straight away rather than when they ring.

The third classic is the paper consignment note going missing. The solution is to capture the consignment note and POD digitally the moment delivery is completed and attach them to the order. RAHTIS itself describes how the driver receives the job and status updates directly on their phone and the documents are saved in the system (source).

The fourth problem is the customer ringing with the question "where's the lorry?". When the order status and documents can be shared as a link, you can answer by looking at your own screen. To be honest: if the driver still does not update the status, no system will fix that, so learning the routine is part of getting started.

How do you introduce RR tracking as part of transport management?

The first week in practice

Day one: add your own vehicles and drivers to RAHTIS. Day two: take one real job from the freight exchange and run it through the system from collection to POD, without duplicating it on paper. Day three: send the customer the first tracking link and ask whether it looks like what they need. Rest of the week: move the remaining active jobs into the system and deliberately put the notebook aside. If something breaks, fix it in the system rather than going back to the old way.

In a small firm the responsibilities are clear: whoever accepts the job marks its status. The driver updates collection and delivery; you confirm the consignment note and invoicing. One rule is enough: the status changes only in the system, not by agreeing over the phone to do it "later".

Where RAHTIS is enough and where it is not

RAHTIS is enough for what most firms with 1–12 vehicles need RR tracking for: the order is tracked stage by stage from collection to delivery, the customer sees the status of their own job without calling, and filling empty legs happens in the same place as dispatch. It does not replace a GPS tracker fitted to the vehicle, so real-time map position and vehicle data come from elsewhere if you want them. Nor is it a full accounting program, although invoicing and payment tracking are covered. An honest test: if your customers demand minute-by-minute real-time location or ERP integrations, you need a bigger system alongside it. If what you need is for jobs to progress visibly without phone calls, this is enough.

FAQ

How much does RR tracking cost a small haulage firm?

The cost depends on the system, but order-based tracking is typically much cheaper than a GPS solution fitted to the vehicle, because it needs no devices, installation or maintenance. In RAHTIS, tracking is part of the order workflow, so there is no separate tracking charge. When comparing, also count the time saved: fewer calls and notes mean fewer working hours.

Can RR tracking be done without a driver app?

Yes, but it shifts the work to the transport planner. Someone has to update the statuses, and if the driver does not do it from their phone, you mark collections, swaps and deliveries yourself based on reports from the road. This works with a small number of jobs, but a good part of the benefit is lost: statuses lag and the customer's visibility suffers. In practice an app for the driver is the simplest way to keep the information up to date.

Does order tracking also work for one-off jobs taken from a freight exchange?

Yes, and that is where it is most useful. A job taken from a freight exchange gets its own reference, around which collection, load confirmation, any swap and delivery with POD build up. A task published in RAHTIS goes straight into your own workflow without separate records or copying into a spreadsheet. The customer sees the stages of their own consignment even if the same lorry carries several different loads in the course of the day.

How are the POD and consignment note made part of tracking?

The delivery stage is confirmed with a POD: a receipt, signature or photo is attached directly to the order the moment the delivery is completed. That way the paper consignment note does not go missing, and the consignment note, POD and invoicing stay in the same record. Invoicing moves forward automatically with the delivery, and the documents can be shared with the customer as a link without chasing email attachments afterwards.

Does RR tracking need a separate GPS tracker in the vehicle?

No. Order tracking is based on stage updates recorded by the driver or transport planner along the way, so nothing is fitted to the vehicle. A GPS unit is only worthwhile if your customers require real-time lorry location in the contract, you need maintenance or working time data, or your fleet is so spread out that a fleet manager's view is essential. For most firms with 1–12 vehicles, status information is enough for their customers.
